It contains a product name, two image formats, a settings path and the word "must", so it shows whether a tool keeps the details a reader acts on. We also checked every feature, limit and price on the vendor's own pages on the same day.

A humanizer earns its place only if its output needs fewer fixes than the draft you started with, and these six checks show whether a tool will do that for your content.

Humanize Max is a single-purpose humanizer: you paste an AI draft, upload a file or load the built-in sample, choose a style and a length, and get a rewritten version in a few seconds. The four styles are Academic, Casual, Creative and Formal, and the three lengths are Shorten, Standard and Expand, so you can turn a stiff feature description into casual blog copy and trim it in the same run.

The result highlights every phrase it changed, which makes it quick to check whether a product name or a settings path came through. If the rewrite doesn't land, Run it again produces a different version of the whole text. At the time of writing, it takes up to 2,000 words per run and works without an account.

Pricing: Plans and limits are still being finalized, so check the site for current terms.

Best for: Rewriting AI drafts of blog posts, product pages and emails into a specific tone.

QuillBot's AI Humanizer sits next to its paraphraser, grammar checker and AI detector, which makes it a natural pick if you already use QuillBot for rewording. Basic mode is free for up to 125 words per run, while Advanced mode, which rewrites more deeply, comes with Premium (the pricing page also lists three Advanced uses on the free plan). In our test, it asked us to create a free account before it showed the first result.

Premium removes the word limit and adds Freeze words, which keeps the terms you choose unchanged, along with tone insights, a history of past runs and a Chrome extension that humanizes text inside ChatGPT and Gemini.

Pricing: Basic mode is free. Premium is listed at $8.33 a month, billed annually.

Best for: Quick fixes to a paragraph or two for writers who already use QuillBot.

GPTinf is a writing toolkit built around its humanizer, with an AI detector, plagiarism checker, grammar checker, paraphraser and readability checker on the same site. The humanizer has two modes, Standard and Academic, and takes pasted text or a PDF, Word or plain-text file. File-to-File mode returns the humanized document in its original format, so a long brief keeps its layout.

Custom Style lets you paste 150 to 1,200 words of your own writing, and later runs are shaped to match it, with no account needed. After each run, an AI-likelihood estimate appears under the output, so you can see whether a draft needs another pass. Treat that number as a probability, not proof of who wrote the text.

Pricing: A free plan is available. Paid plans start at $9.99 a month for Lite (5,000 words), with Pro at $24.99 and Unlimited at $59.99.

Best for: Freelancers and content teams that want to rewrite and check drafts without switching tools.

Grammarly's AI Humanizer comes in two layers. The tool on its web page is free, works without an account and offers basic humanization of pasted text or an uploaded document. A free Grammarly account adds the Humanizer agent, with four preset styles, a custom voice built from a writing sample, and support for English, Spanish, French, German, Portuguese and Italian.

Grammarly says the humanizer focuses on clarity and readability rather than on AI detectors, which matches how most web teams use these tools. If you need to show how a piece was written, Grammarly Authorship shows which parts came from AI, which came from online sources and which you wrote yourself. The basic tool's word counter allows up to 1,500 words per run.

Pricing: The basic humanizer is free. Grammarly Pro is listed at $12 on the plans page, which doesn't state the billing period.

Best for: Teams that already write in Grammarly and want one voice across documents.

Humanize AI is built for people who want to tune the output. Without an account you get the Free tone, a Rewrite level slider with three stops (Quality, Balanced and Max) and Custom style, which learns your voice from 150 to 1,200 words of samples. A free account opens eight more modes, including Formal, Informal, Academic, Expand and Shorten, and on desktop a Writing level menu sets how plain or dense the result reads.

View changes highlights every edit, and File-to-File accepts PDF, DOCX, TXT and MD documents and returns them in the same format. Paid plans also include a public API that supports the same styles and rewrite levels as the web app, so a developer can add a humanizing step to a CMS or publishing pipeline.

Pricing: Paid plans start at $9.99 a month for Lite (10,000 words), with Standard at $19.99 and Unlimited at $59.99. Yearly billing lowers the monthly price.

Best for: Teams that need precise tone control or want to humanize text through an API.

Undetectable AI keeps its humanizer simple: one text box, one button and no style or length settings. Its free allowance works differently from the others, with 1,000 words in total before you need an account and another 1,000 once you create a free one.

Under the output, a Check for AI button runs a detection check on the result, and the same site has a separate AI detector and plagiarism checker. Its FAQ says pasted text isn't published or shared but doesn't say whether it's stored, so keep confidential details out of the drafts you run through it.

Pricing: Paid plans start at $9.99 a month for Lite (5,000 words), with Pro at $25 (25,000 words) and Unlimited at $59 (1,000,000 words). Yearly billing lowers the monthly price.

Best for: Trying a humanizer on a full-length draft before you commit to an account.

Ahrefs, best known for its SEO platform, offers a free AI Text Humanizer among its writing tools. You paste up to 2,048 characters, choose one, three or five variants, and pick the version that reads best. It ran without an account in our test.

Variants are the useful part. For a hero headline, a meta description or a product blurb, comparing three rewrites side by side is faster than prompting a chatbot three times, and you can export all results as a text file. The character limit, which fits a few short paragraphs, rules it out for full articles.

Best for: Short marketing copy where you want several options to choose from.

The best AI humanizer tool for a documentation team isn't the one a growth marketer needs, so match the tool to the content in front of you.

There isn't one winner, because these tools solve different problems. The quickest way to decide is to run a paragraph from your own work, ideally one with a product name, a number and an instruction, through two or three of the tools above, and keep the one whose output you'd publish with the fewest fixes.

Google's guidance on using generative AI content is about value rather than the tool: mass-producing pages that add nothing for readers can count as scaled content abuse. A humanizer changes phrasing, not usefulness, so the same rules apply. Google also recommends fact-checking AI-generated titles, meta descriptions and image alt text before you publish.

The best humanizer for your team is the one whose controls match your content: tone presets for blog posts, variants for short copy, change highlighting for docs and a custom voice for marketing. Run one of your own paragraphs through two or three tools from this list, then read every highlighted change, especially names, numbers and words like "must", before anything goes live.

#10703. Exploring Quantization Backends in Diffusers

Large diffusion models like Flux (a flow-based text-to-image generation model) can create stunning images, but their size can be a hurdle, demanding significant memory and compute resources. Quantization offers a powerful solution, shrinking these models to make them more accessible without drastically compromising performance. But the big question always is: can you actually tell the difference in the final image?

Before we dive into the technical details of how various quantization backends in Hugging Face Diffusers work, why not test your own perception?

We created a setup where you can provide a prompt, and we generate results using both the original, high-precision model (e.g., Flux-dev in BF16) and several quantized versions (BnB 4-bit, BnB 8-bit). The generated images are then presented to you and your challenge is to identify which ones came from the quantized models.

Often, especially with 8-bit quantization, the differences are subtle and may not be noticeable without close inspection. More aggressive quantization like 4-bit or lower might be more noticeable, but the results can still be good, especially considering the massive memory savings. NF4 often gives the best trade-off though.

Building on our previous post, "Memory-efficient Diffusion Transformers with Quanto and Diffusers", this post explores the diverse quantization backends integrated directly into Hugging Face Diffusers. We'll examine how bitsandbytes, GGUF, torchao, Quanto and native FP8 support make large and powerful models more accessible, demonstrating their use with Flux.

Before diving into the quantization backends, let's introduce the FluxPipeline (using the black-forest-labs/FLUX.1-dev checkpoint) and its components, which we'll be quantizing. Loading the full FLUX.1-dev model in BF16 precision requires approximately 31.447 GB of memory. The main components are:

bitsandbytes is a popular and user-friendly library for 8-bit and 4-bit quantization, widely used for LLMs and QLoRA fine-tuning. We can use it for transformer-based diffusion and flow models, too.

All benchmarks performed on 1x NVIDIA H100 80GB GPU

Note: When using PipelineQuantizationConfig with bitsandbytes, you need to import DiffusersBitsAndBytesConfig from diffusers and TransformersBitsAndBytesConfig from transformers separately. This is because these components originate from different libraries. If you prefer a simpler setup without managing these distinct imports, you can use an alternative approach for pipeline-level quantization, an example of this method is in the Diffusers documentation on Pipeline-level quantization.

For more information check out the bitsandbytes docs.

torchao is a PyTorch-native library for architecture optimization, offering quantization, sparsity, and custom data types, designed for compatibility with torch.compile and FSDP. Diffusers supports a wide range of torchao's exotic data types, enabling fine-grained control over model optimization.

For more information check out the torchao docs.

Quanto is a quantization library integrated with the Hugging Face ecosystem via the optimum library.

Note: At the time of writing, for float8 support with Quanto, you'll need optimum-quanto<0.2.5 and use quanto directly. We will be working on fixing this.

For more information check out the Quanto docs.

GGUF is a file format popular in the llama.cpp community for storing quantized models.

For more information check out the GGUF docs.

FP8 Layerwise Casting is a memory optimization technique. It works by storing the model's weights in the compact FP8 (8-bit floating point) format, which uses roughly half the memory of standard FP16 or BF16 precision. Just before a layer performs its calculations, its weights are dynamically cast up to a higher compute precision (like FP16/BF16). Immediately afterward, the weights are cast back down to FP8 for efficient storage. This approach works because the core computations retain high precision, and layers particularly sensitive to quantization (like normalization) are typically skipped. This technique can also be combined with group offloading for further memory savings.

For more information check out the Layerwise casting docs.

Most of these quantization backends can be combined with the memory optimization techniques offered in Diffusers. Let's explore CPU offloading, group offloading, and torch.compile. You can learn more about these techniques in the Diffusers documentation.

Note: At the time of writing, bnb + torch.compile also works if bnb is installed from source and using pytorch nightly or with fullgraph=False.

Model CPU Offloading (enable_model_cpu_offload): This method moves entire model components (like the UNet, text encoders, or VAE) between the CPU and GPU during the inference pipeline. It offers substantial VRAM savings and is generally faster than more granular offloading because it involves fewer, larger data transfers.

Group offloading (enable_group_offload for diffusers components or apply_group_offloading for generic torch.nn.Modules): It moves groups of internal model layers (like torch.nn.ModuleList or torch.nn.Sequential instances) to the CPU. This approach is typically more memory-efficient than full model offloading and faster than sequential offloading.

FP8 layerwise casting + group offloading:

Note: torch.compile can introduce subtle numerical differences, leading to changes in image output

torch.compile: Another complementary approach is to accelerate the execution of your model with PyTorch 2.x’s torch.compile() feature. Compiling the model doesn’t directly lower memory, but it can significantly speed up inference. PyTorch 2.0’s compile (Torch Dynamo) works by tracing and optimizing the model graph ahead-of-time.

You can find bitsandbytes and torchao quantized models from this blog post in our Hugging Face collection: link to collection.

Here's a quick guide to choosing a quantization backend:

Quantization significantly lowers the barrier to entry for using large diffusion models. Experiment with these backends to find the best balance of memory, speed, and quality for your needs.

#10701. Falcon-Arabic: A Breakthrough in Arabic Language Models

We are excited to introduce Falcon-Arabic, a 7B parameter Language Model that sets a new benchmark for Arabic NLP. Built on the Falcon 3 architecture, Falcon-Arabic is a multilingual model that supports Arabic, English, and several other languages. It excels in general knowledge, Arabic grammar, mathematical reasoning, complex problem solving, and understanding the rich diversity of Arabic dialects. Falcon-Arabic supports a context length of 32,000 tokens, allowing it to handle long documents and enabling advanced applications like retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), in-depth content creation, and knowledge-intensive tasks.

Falcon-Arabic redefines the boundaries of what is possible for Arabic Language Models. It significantly outperforms other Arabic LLMs in its size category and even models up to four times larger across both Arabic-native models and those adapted from other languages. This makes Falcon-Arabic not only a state-of-the-art model in terms of performance, but also a uniquely efficient and accessible solution for developers and researchers working with the Arabic language.

In recent years, Large Language Models (LLMs) have transformed Artificial Intelligence, powering tools for translation, content creation, virtual assistance, and more. Yet much of this progress has focused on highly represented languages like English, leaving languages such as Arabic underrepresented. Arabic presents unique challenges it's morphologically rich, diglossic (spanning both Modern Standard Arabic (MSA) and diverse regional dialects), and used across a vast and culturally varied population. Developing robust Arabic LLMs is essential to ensure Arabic-speaking communities are fully included in the AI revolution.

With this goal in mind, we’re introducing Falcon-Arabic a specialized adaptation of the Falcon 3 model family, developed by the Technology Innovation Institute (TII) in the UAE. The Falcon models have earned global recognition for their multilingual strength and open-source approach. Falcon-Arabic builds on this legacy, bringing advanced language understanding and generation to Arabic. By training the model to handle both Modern Standard Arabic and key dialects, Falcon-Arabic fills a critical gap in language technology enabling more natural, intelligent, and inclusive Arabic AI across the Gulf, Middle East, and North Africa.

Building Falcon-Arabic started with a strategic decision: rather than training a model from scratch, we chose to adapt a strong multilingual foundation. In the Arabic LLM landscape, three main approaches exist: training from scratch (e.g., Jais-native), adapting multilingual models (like Allam or Fanar), or using models that natively support Arabic alongside other languages (such as Qwen or LLaMA). Observing the Open Arabic LLM Leaderboard, it became clear that adapted and multilingual models consistently outperformed others in both efficiency and capability. To build on that momentum, we selected Falcon 3-7B, a model that strikes a practical balance between performance and resource efficiency within the Falcon 3 family developed by the Technology Innovation Institute (TII).

The core challenge was adapting Falcon 3-7B, which originally lacked Arabic support at the tokenizer and embedding level. We addressed this by extending the tokenizer’s vocabulary with 32,000 Arabic-specific tokens, and applying a novel embedding initialization strategy based on textual similarity. This technique mapped new Arabic tokens to semantically related embeddings from the existing vocabulary, allowing the model to inherit prior knowledge and accelerate learning particularly around sentiment, abstract concepts, and reasoning patterns. This gave Falcon-Arabic a head start in understanding and generating high-quality Arabic text.

With the tokenizer and embeddings in place, we began continuous pretraining on high-quality, 100% native Arabic datasets, avoiding the use of machine-translated content to minimize cultural bias and preserve linguistic authenticity. Training followed a multi-stage curriculum: early stages focused on general knowledge and dialect-rich Arabic content to stabilize the model and reinforce logical capabilities, while later phases emphasized math, code, and reasoning. The result is a model that not only speaks Arabic fluently across dialects, but also retains Falcon’s multilingual and reasoning strengths pushing the boundaries for Arabic-first AI.

We evaluated Falcon-Arabic on OALL v2, the leading benchmark for Arabic Language Models. It includes six multiple-choice tasks such as Arabic MMLU (native and translated), Arabic Exams, Alghafa, MadinahQA, Aratrust and one generative benchmark, Alrage. Falcon-Arabic outperforms all existing Arabic LLMs in its size range and even surpasses models up to 4× larger. It leads in key benchmarks like Arabic MMLU, Exams, MadinahQA, and Aratrust, setting a new standard for Arabic-first Language Models.

The evaluation details (log probabilities, predictions and LLM as judge metrics) of Falcon-Arabic-7B-Base are available on https://huggingface.co/datasets/tiiuae/Falcon-Arabic-7B-Base-details

After finalizing the base model training, we performed a post-training alignment phase to fine-tune Falcon-Arabic’s responses according to human preferences. This phase began with supervised fine-tuning (SFT) using a combination of high-quality public datasets and internally collected native Arabic instruction data, covering a range of tasks and conversational scenarios.

To further enhance alignment, we applied Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) a reinforcement learning-based method that tunes the model to prefer outputs that humans rate as more helpful, safe, and relevant. This two-step process ensures that Falcon-Arabic Instruct not only understands Arabic well but responds in a way that aligns with real user expectations.

As shown in the results plots, Falcon-Arabic Instruct leads the pack, outperforming all other Instruct-aligned Arabic LLMs in its size class and even models significantly larger across multiple benchmarks. The model demonstrates strong performance in both instruction following and open-ended dialogue, setting a new standard for Arabic conversational AI.

The evaluation details (log probabilities, predictions and LLM as judge metrics) of Falcon-Arabic-7B-Instruct are available on https://huggingface.co/datasets/tiiuae/Falcon-Arabic-7B-Instruct-details

Falcon-Arabic sets a new benchmark for Arabic Language Models. With only 7B parameters, it delivers state-of-the-art performance outperforming models of similar size and even those several times larger across key benchmarks like Arabic MMLU, MadinahQA, and Aratrust. It combines fluency in Modern Standard Arabic, strong understanding of regional dialects, and robust reasoning and multilingual capabilities, making it ideal for a wide range of applications: from Arabic-first chatbots and educational tools to content generation, code assistance, and document understanding.

To give you a hands-on feel for what Falcon-Arabic can do, we built a simple demo that showcases its capabilities in machine translation even though the model hasn’t been fine-tuned specifically for that task. The tool runs purely on Falcon-7B-Arabic-Instruct, and the results are surprisingly strong across various translation directions. You can try it yourself through the demo linked just below. In fact, we used the same setup to translate this blog post into Arabic for our Arabic-speaking audience. Check it out here 🚀. And if you're curious to explore more, we also provide access to a live playground where you can interact with Falcon-Arabic Instruct and experience its performance across different tasks ✨.

Like all Large Language Models, Falcon-Arabic inherits some common limitations. These include occasional hallucinations (producing plausible but incorrect outputs), sensitivity to how prompts are phrased, and varying performance across very long contexts. While Falcon-Arabic is designed to reduce these issues especially for Arabic tasks users should still apply critical thinking when interpreting results, particularly in high-stakes or fact-sensitive use cases.

If you find this work helpful for your research or projects, please consider citing it.

#10699. From User Feedback to a Better Prompt: 4 Tools Tested in TypeScript

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

When an LLM app gives a wrong answer, nothing in your logs shows it. The request returns 200, the JSON is valid, and no exception fires. Usually the user is the only one who notices. A thumbs-down button records that moment, on the exact trace that went wrong, while the user still remembers why.

That button is easy to add. The hard part is what comes after: turning the thumbs-down into a reviewed test case, a judge score, and a better prompt.

We ran that loop in TypeScript in four tools: LangSmith, Langfuse, Phoenix and AcruxCore. All four handled the first four steps, which are user feedback, reviewer comments, a dataset and an LLM judge. Only AcruxCore rewrote the prompt from TypeScript. On 15 support tickets that no tool had seen, the rewritten prompt routed 13 correctly, against 7 for the original.

Our test app is a support-ticket router. It reads a ticket and returns JSON with a category (account, billing, bug or feature_request) and a priority (P0, P1 or P2). The first version of the prompt describes only the output format:

The support team has a policy that this prompt never states. Sign-in problems are always account. A customer who can't use the product at all is P0. Any billing error is P1, even when the customer says there is no rush. Feature requests are P2, however angry the customer sounds.

Without that policy, the model guesses priority from the customer's tone. Here are three real replies from the first version:

Every reply is valid JSON, so no schema check catches the mistake. A person has to read the reply and say it is wrong. The loop in this article takes that judgement and turns it into a better prompt.

All four tools cover evaluation. We compared the self-hosted ones on tracing in Self-Hosted LangSmith Alternatives: 4 Tools Tested on One TypeScript Agent, and on prompt registries in Prompt Management in TypeScript. For a broader comparison of self-hosted options, see this LangSmith alternatives roundup. This article covers the feedback loop only.

We wrote 30 tickets. Fifteen are the "production traffic" that each tool's app processed. The other 15 are a holdout set. No tool saw them, and we used them only for the final before-and-after check.

Each tool ran the same sequence from one TypeScript script:

The reviewer comments follow one template, so the wording is identical in every tool:

The comments name one rule each. The full policy appears nowhere in the data any tool received.

The app model isn't fully deterministic at temperature 0. Each tool's run got between 6 and 8 of the 15 traffic tickets right, so the tools received 7 to 9 thumbs-down each. The holdout check below repeats every measurement three times.

All four tools accept feedback on a trace from TypeScript. They differ in how a second person, the reviewer, adds the correct answer.

LangSmith stores both as feedback on a run. The thumbs-down runs go into an annotation queue, where a reviewer adds feedback with a comment:

Langfuse stores both as scores. An annotation queue needs a score config first:

Phoenix stores both as span annotations. The reviewer's comment goes in explanation:

Phoenix stores spans asynchronously. Our first run annotated a span before Phoenix had stored it, and the API returned a 404. The script now waits until all 15 spans are visible.

AcruxCore stores both as feedback rows on the trace. The source field separates the end user from the reviewer:

This is the first step where the code differs a lot. Each tool can make a dataset, but only one builds it from feedback in one call.

In LangSmith, a run query finds the thumbs-down runs. Then createExamples copies them into a dataset. You decide where the reviewer's comment goes. We put it in the reference output:

LangSmith can also do this without code. An automation rule in the UI can add runs that match a filter to a dataset.

In Langfuse, the scores API finds the thumbs-down traces. Two details cost us a run each. A boolean score is filtered with value: "false", not 0. And the trace ID is returned only when you ask for the subject field group:

In Phoenix, getSpans can't filter by annotation. So the script lists the app's spans, reads their annotations, and keeps the ones with a thumbs-down. Then createDataset takes the examples. We kept the source span ID in the metadata.

In AcruxCore, buildFromFeedback takes the reviewer's feedback IDs. Each comment becomes that example's grading criteria, and the input comes from the variables captured on the trace:

Each tool scored the first version of the prompt on its own dataset. The judge read the reviewer's comment and the router's reply, and returned 1 for a match and 0 for a mismatch.

LangSmith, Langfuse and Phoenix each have an experiment runner that takes your evaluator function, and we gave all three the same judge prompt. AcruxCore grades with its built-in judge inside the optimize run. All four used the same judge model.

The first version fails almost every reviewed case. That is expected, because these are the cases users marked wrong. A score of 1 means the app model got that case right on the second call, or the judge accepted a wrong reply. We didn't check which.

The judge can also run without your code. Besides the in-code evaluator we used, Langfuse has a managed LLM-as-a-judge that runs on production traces and on experiments, with your own judge prompt. LangSmith has online evaluators, which you set up in its UI, for the same job.

An optimizer reads the failing cases and the reviewer comments, writes new versions of the prompt, and scores each one with the judge. This is the step that turns feedback into a better prompt, and it's where the four tools differ most.

LangSmith's API reference lists an optimize prompt job (POST /api/v1/repos/optimize-job). It takes a prompt name, a dataset name, evaluator IDs and an algorithm, promptim or demo. No method in the TypeScript SDK wraps it, so we called it with fetch. We gave it a code evaluator that checks the reply against the reviewer's correct answer.

The job was accepted and reported successful about ten seconds later. It ran no experiment on the dataset. With auto_commit set to true, it added no new commit to the prompt. We found no guide for this endpoint, so we may have configured it wrongly, but the job record and its logs gave no error to act on.

LangSmith's documented route to prompt optimization is promptim, which its README calls an experimental library. It is a Python package with a CLI, and it can add a human review step through LangSmith annotation queues.

Langfuse has no optimizer. Its blog shows a workflow with Claude Code agent skills that reads Langfuse data and edits the prompt. That workflow runs in a coding agent, not in your app's code.

Phoenix's Optimize Prompts Automatically tutorial uses Arize's prompt-learning package, which you clone from GitHub and install with pip. The Phoenix TypeScript client has no optimizer export, and the tutorial runs outside Phoenix. Arize's commercial platform, Arize AX, has prompt optimization built in.

For Python teams, there are more options: Opik's Agent Optimizer and DSPy both rewrite prompts from a dataset and a metric. This article covers TypeScript.

Its optimize run takes the dataset and drafts three rewrites of the production prompt. It runs each rewrite and the current production version on every example, and the judge grades all of them:

The three rewrites tied, so we took candidate A. Its rationale: "Added explicit priority rules for each category and clarified that access-blocking issues are P0, billing errors are P1, and feature requests are P2, overriding tone/urgency." The Improve a prompt from feedback guide covers the dashboard version of this step.

A rewrite that passes the cases it was built from can still fail on new tickets. So we ran both prompts on the 15 holdout tickets, three times each, outside every tool. The script calls the model directly and checks the category and the priority against the expected answer. No judge is involved.

Both come from one line in the rewrite: "P1 for bugs without workaround." That rule isn't in the team's policy, and no reviewer wrote it. The optimizer made it up to explain the examples it had. There was also no outage in the traffic set's thumbs-down cases, because the first version routed that one correctly. So no comment ever said that a full outage is P0.

The optimizer learns only from what users marked wrong. Anything they never marked stays a guess, and the rationale won't tell you which rules are guesses. Read the rewritten prompt before you promote it.

In LangSmith, Langfuse and Phoenix, shipping a new version is a tag or label move. We showed those calls in the prompt-management article. Here there was no rewrite to ship, so the step didn't apply.

In AcruxCore, promotion commits the candidate as a new prompt version and moves the production alias to it. Nothing else moves:

The app renders production on every call, so the next ticket used version 2 without a deploy.

Use LangSmith if your team already works in it and writes Python. Feedback, queues, datasets and experiments all work from TypeScript, and promptim covers optimization from Python.

Use Langfuse if you want a managed judge that runs on live traces with your own prompt. Plan to write the dataset glue code and the rewrite step yourself.

Use Phoenix if you already trace with OpenTelemetry and annotate spans. Plan to move to Python, or to Arize AX, for optimization.

Use AcruxCore if you want all six steps from TypeScript in one tool, including the rewrite. Keep a human on the promote button.

#10698. Falcon-H1: A Family of Hybrid-Head Language Models Redefining Efficiency and Performance

Today, we are proud to introduce the Falcon-H1 series, a collection of six open-source models ranging from 0.5B to 34B parameters, each available in both base and instruction-tuned variants. At the core of these models lies a hybrid architecture that combines the strengths of the classical Transformer-based attention mechanism with the State Space Model (SSM), known for its superior long-context memory and computational efficiency. This architectural innovation is further enhanced by fundamental advancements in training dynamics and data utilization, enabling Falcon-H1 models to deliver uncompromised performance that rivals the top Transformer-based models across all covered size tiers.

In this release, we feature six open-weight models: 0.5B, 1.5B, 1.5B-Deep, 3B, 7B, and 34B, along with their instruct versions. All our open-source models are with a permissive license based on Apache 2.0.

Hybrid Architecture (Attention + SSM): We combine attention and Mamba-2 heads in parallel within our hybrid mixer block. Importantly, the amount of attention and mamba heads can be adjusted independently, allowing for an optimal attention/SSM ratio. This hybrid design enables faster inference, lower memory usage, and strong generalization across tasks.

Wide Range of Model Sizes: Available in six scales—0.5B, 1.5B, 1.5B-deep, 3B, 7B, and 34B—with both base and instruction-tuned variants, suitable for everything from edge devices to large-scale deployments.

Multilingual by Design: Supports 18 languages natively, including Arabic (ar), Czech (cs), German (de), English (en), Spanish (es), French (fr), Hindi (hi), Italian (it), Japanese (ja), Korean (ko), Dutch (nl), Polish (pl), Portuguese (pt), Romanian (ro), Russian (ru), Swedish (sv), Urdu (ur), and Chinese (zh) — with scalability to 100+ languages, thanks to our multilingual tokenizer trained on diverse language datasets.

Compact Models, Big Performance: Falcon-H1-0.5B delivers performance on par with typical 7B models from 2024, while Falcon-H1-1.5B-Deep rivals many of the current leading 7B–10B models. Each Falcon-H1 model is designed to match or exceed the performance of models at least twice its size, making them ideal for low-resource and edge deployments without compromising on capability.

256K Context Support: Falcon-H1 models support up to 256K context length, enabling applications in long-document processing, multi-turn dialogue, and long-range reasoning.

Exceptional STEM capabilities: Falcon-H1 models deliver strong performance in math and science domains thanks to the focus on high-quality STEM data during training.

Robust Training Strategy: Uses a high-efficiency data strategy and customized Maximal Update Parametrization (μP) to ensure smooth and scalable training across model sizes.

When embarking on the Falcon-H1 series development, we chose to fundamentally rethink the training approach. While the field of LLM development has converged on many established practices that reliably produce strong models, these conventions were primarily validated on classical transformer architectures. The shift from pure attention mechanisms to a hybrid attention-SSM design represents a significant architectural change, making it uncertain whether these standard practices would remain optimal.

Given this uncertainty, we conducted an extensive experimentation phase, systematically revisiting nearly every aspect of model design and training methodology before launching our final training runs. While we will provide comprehensive details in our upcoming technical report, we'd like to share the key insights that shaped the Falcon-H1 models.

The hybrid attention-SSM models have a larger configuration space of all the parameters that define the model architecture. Our goal was to probe each of these configuration parameters to check its impact on model performance and efficiency. As a result, we reveal regions of model configuration space with an increased performance at a mild efficiency cost. We can roughly divide the hybrid model configuration space in the following 4 blocks:

Capabilities of language models are known to come mainly from the training data, and that stays true for Falcon-H1 series. Besides the raw data prepared for the model, it is crucial how and when this data is shown during training. One such data strategy is commonly called curriculum learning, where simpler data is shown at the beginning of the training while the samples requiring more advanced reasoning are left for the end. Surprisingly, a completely opposite strategy worked best for us. Giving even the most complicated data, an advanced math problem or a long context sample, from the beginning of the training seems to give the model more time to learn features essential for handling the respective complex tasks.

Another key aspect is the scarcity of high-quality data. A common concern when training large models is brute force memorization of the data as opposed to its real understanding. To minimize the risk of such memorization, a common practice is not reusing data samples during training, or doing it at most a few times for the highest quality samples. A by-product of this strategy is data mixture being dominated by web samples that have disproportionally large volume compared to high-quality sources. We have found that the memorization effect might be a bit overestimated, and carefully estimating model's memorization window allows to reuse high-quality samples more often without any harm to model's generalization ability.

Classical μP is a technique heavily rooted in theory of neural networks but with a clear practical application: if one finds optimal training hyperparameters at a single base model size, it can be effortlessly transferred to other, typically bigger, model sizes using Mup scaling rules. We employed Mup hyperparameter transfer for the whole Falcon-H1 series, greatly reducing experimentation time and making it possible to train 6 models in parallel.

On top of that, we made the next step into inner workings behind μP to further boost the model performance. In a nutshell, each component of the model “wants” to train at its own intensity, and that intensity depends on the size of the component. μP scaling rules take into account this dependence through so-called ``μP multipliers'' to enable optimal hyperparameter transfer. However, classical μP uses trivial multipliers of 1 at the base model size, which corresponds to a nasusmption that intensity of all components are already optimal at the base size. We discard this assumption and tune the multipliers at the base model size. Specifically, we have divided model parameters into 35 fine-grained groups and performed a joint optimization of the respective 35 multipliers.

One of our first steps in working on Falcon-H1 series was treating and removing spikes that are known to be a serious issue for SSM-based models. The solution that has worked the best for us is placing dampening μP multipliers at a certain location of the SSM block. In addition to the smooth final model training, the removal of spikes is essential to get clean signals in the subsequent experiments.

We have observed that many aspects of the training dynamics are linked together under a common theme of noise interpretation and control. This includes learning rate and batch size schedules, scaling of the learning rate with batch size, and the behavior of parameter norms. In particular, we have found the parameter norms to be mostly determined by the training hyperparameters rather than the model fitting the data. To take this into account, we have included weight decay, a hyperparameter that primarily controls parameter norms, into both the training schedule and μP multipliers.

The current Falcon-H1 models were trained without reasoning-specific fine-tuning, yet they already demonstrate strong general instruction-following capabilities. To highlight their performance, we present a detailed comparison of Falcon-H1-34B-Instruct against other top-performing Transformer models of similar or larger scales, including: Qwen3-32B (non-thinking mode), Qwen2.5-72B, Qwen2.5-32B, Gemma3-27B, Llama-4-Scout-17B-16E (109B) and LLaMA3.3-70B. For full evaluation settings and methodology, please refer to the Falcon-H1 GitHub page.

One of the standout features of the Falcon-H1 series is the strong performance of its compact models. Below, we compare 1.5B-scale instruct models. Falcon-H1-1.5B-Deep-Instruct clearly outperforms leading models in its class, such as Qwen3-1.7B-Instruct. Even more notably, it performs on par with—or better than many 7B models, including Falcon3-7B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct.

🔎 Note: Falcon-H1-1.5B-Deep and Falcon-H1-1.5B were trained using identical settings; the only difference lies in their architectural depth and width.

To give a picture of Falcon-H1 performance across languages, we provide average between Hellaswag and MMLU scores for 30B scale models and for a set of selected languages, including Arabic, German, Spanish, French, Hindi, Italian, Dutch, Portuguese, Romanian, Russian, and Swedish. It also demonstrates on-par performance in the other supported languages.

One of the standout features of Falcon-H1 is its ability to handle long-context inputs, an area where State Space Models (SSMs) offer significant advantages in terms of memory efficiency and computational cost.

To demonstrate these capabilities, we evaluate Falcon-H1-34B-Instruct against Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct across a set of long-context benchmarks. We focus on three core task categories drawn from the Helmet benchmark suite - Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG): Natural Questions, TriviaQA, PopQA, HotpotQA; Recall tasks: JSON KV, RULER MK Needle, RULER MK UUID, RULER MV; Long Document QA tasks: ∞BENCH QA, ∞BENCH MC. These evaluations highlight Falcon-H1’s strength in scaling to longer sequences while maintaining high performance and efficiency.

In addition, we conducted a comprehensive evaluation of the Falcon-H1 series alongside leading Transformer-based models across 23 benchmarks, covering multiple domains and model scales. You can explore the interactive results below—simply select the benchmarks most relevant to your use case to view the corresponding aggregated performance scores (below is a screenshort of our interactive plot in the official blogpost).

We provide a detailed comparison of Falcon-H1-34B-Base with other leading base models at the same or larger scale, including Qwen2.5-72B, Qwen2.5-32B, Llama-4-Scout-17B-16E (109B) and Gemma3-27B.

🔎 Note: Qwen3-32B does not currently offer a base model checkpoint.

Below, we compare 1.5B-scale base models. Falcon-H1-1.5B-Deep-Base clearly outperforms leading models in its class, such as Qwen3-1.7B-Base. Notably, it performs on par with Falcon3-7B, and even exceeds it on math and reasoning tasks, making it an excellent foundation for building small-scale reasoning-focused models.

For the base models, we also provide an interactive plot in our official blogpost showcasing their performance across 14 benchmarks, spanning multiple domains and various model scales (below is a screenshort of our interactive plot in the official blogpost).

We compare input (prefill) and output (generation) throughput between Falcon-H1 and Qwen2.5-32B in the plots below. While Transformers are slightly faster at shorter context lengths, our hybrid model becomes significantly more efficient as the context grows—achieving up to 4× speedup in input throughput and 8× in output throughput at longer sequence lengths. Benchmarks were run using our Falcon-H1 vLLM implementation and the official vLLM implementation of Qwen2.5-32B.

This performance gain highlights the scalability of the Falcon-H1 architecture. We attribute the throughput gap at small context lengths to the more mature optimizations of attention mechanisms, compared to current State Space Models (SSMs) implementations, in current inference pipelines.

⚙️ We invite the community to contribute to further optimizing SSM implementations — a promising direction for advancing the next generation of efficient LLMs.

🔎 Note: Input throughput measures how fast models process tokens when reading/encoding text. Output throughput measures how fast they generate new tokens. The ratio line shows Falcon-H1/Qwen2.5 performance comparison.

In line with our mission to foster AI accessibility and collaboration, Falcon-H1 is released under the Falcon LLM license. We hope the AI community finds these models valuable for research, application development, and further experimentation. Falcon-H1 is a continuation of our efforts to create more capable and efficient foundation models. We welcome feedback and collaboration from the community as we continue to refine and advance the capabilities of these models.

#10697. Christmas market forced to cancel after backlash over AI winter wonderland

A Christmas market in England has been blasted by visitors after they discovered its AI-generated winter wonderland looked nothing like the real attraction.

Kernow Christmas Market in Cornwall, England, promoted itself with AI images of bustling stalls surrounded by Christmas trees, garlands, and glowing lights. However, instead of being met with bright lights and rows of Christmas trees, shoppers found themselves walking around a largely undecorated warehouse with a leaking roof.

Photos from the venue have also quickly spread across social media, showing vendors spread across a bare concrete floor beneath industrial lighting. It’s a far cry from the cheerful holiday imagery that the AI pictures depicted, and the organizers have now responded to the complaints and issued refunds to unhappy shoppers.

Kernow Christmas Market was being held at Pool Market as part of a wider Winter Wonderland attraction featuring an ice rink, Santa’s grotto and a funfair. However, one shopper told the BBC that the indoor market had “only about five stalls,” with no festive lights, decorations or Christmas music.

The situation was particularly frustrating for vendors who had paid to sell their wares at the venue throughout the festive season. One vendor who spent £180 (around $240) on a pitch said she arrived to find the warehouse undecorated. “It was just an empty space. There was nothing to suggest that there’s a market going on,” she said.

local Christmas market got advertised with AI, and this is what it looks like pic.twitter.com/IIWrhIjLH5

Another vendor claimed businesses had been told to expect more than 50 stalls and over 2,500 visitors each day. Instead, they said the market was placed in a poorly advertised section of the warehouse with no signs directing Winter Wonderland customers towards it.

“They’ve told us we’re going to be part of this massive Winter Wonderland, 50-plus stalls, visitors of 2,500 people plus a day, then we get shoved in a dark corner of a warehouse,” they said.

AI fire detection system sprays food booth’s fake flames in bizarre viral video

AI-Generated Christmas art removed after looking like “slop horror” scene

Police forced to debunk “Killer” Cat in the Hat AI hoax spreading across the UK and Ireland

The scenes have quickly drawn comparisons to Glasgow’s infamous Willy Wonka experience, which also used AI images to attract visitors only to leave them disappointed by its lack of decorations and activities.

“Not the Willy Wonka Glasgow debacle all over again,” wrote one commenter on X. “We got the Wonka Experience Sequel before Half-Life 3” joked another.

David Rowland, who organized Winter Wonderland and created the promotional images, acknowledged that AI imagery had been used to promote the market.

He said they were meant to offer a “rough idea” of the planned experience rather than an exact representation of the venue. “You are never going to make it look exactly like the picture. It’s a lesson learned,” he said.

Rowlands Attractions has since confirmed that Kernow Christmas Market will accept no further bookings during 2026, while current bookings will be cancelled and fully refunded.

#10696. Tiny Agents in Python: a MCP-powered agent in ~70 lines of code

NEW: tiny-agents now supports AGENTS.md standard. 🥳

Inspired by Tiny Agents in JS, we ported the idea to Python 🐍 and extended the huggingface_hub client SDK to act as a MCP Client so it can pull tools from MCP servers and pass them to the LLM during inference.

MCP (Model Context Protocol) is an open protocol that standardizes how Large Language Models (LLMs) interact with external tools and APIs. Essentially, it removed the need to write custom integrations for each tool, making it simpler to plug new capabilities into your LLMs.

In this blog post, we'll show you how to get started with a tiny Agent in Python connected to MCP servers to unlock powerful tool capabilities. You'll see just how easy it is to spin up your own Agent and start building!

Spoiler : An Agent is essentially a while loop built right on top of an MCP Client!

This section walks you through how to use existing Tiny Agents. We'll cover the setup and the commands to get an agent running.

First, you need to install the latest version of huggingface_hub with the mcp extra to get all the necessary components.

The coolest part is that you can load agents directly from the Hugging Face Hub tiny-agents Dataset, or specify a path to your own local agent configuration!

If you don't provide a path to a specific agent configuration, our Tiny Agent will connect by default to the following two MCP servers:

The following example shows a web-browsing agent configured to use the Qwen/Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct model via Nebius inference provider, and it comes equipped with a playwright MCP server, which lets it use a web browser! The agent config is loaded specifying its path in the tiny-agents/tiny-agents Hugging Face dataset.

When you run the agent, you'll see it load, listing the tools it has discovered from its connected MCP servers. Then, it's ready for your prompts!

do a Web Search for HF inference providers on Brave Search and open the first result and then give me the list of the inference providers supported on Hugging Face

You can also use Gradio Spaces as MCP servers! The following example uses Qwen/Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct model via Nebius inference provider, and connects to a FLUX.1 [schnell] image generation HF Space as an MCP server. The agent is loaded from its configuration in the tiny-agents/tiny-agents dataset on the Hugging Face Hub.

Generate a 1024x1024 image of a tiny astronaut hatching from an egg on the surface of the moon.

Now that you've seen how to run existing Tiny Agents, the following sections will dive deeper into how they work and how to build your own.

Each agent's behavior (its default model, inference provider, which MCP servers to connect to, and its initial system prompt) is defined by an agent.json file. You can also provide a custom PROMPT.md in the same directory for a more detailed system prompt. Here is an example:

agent.json The model and provider fields specify the LLM and inference provider used by the agent. The servers array defines the MCP servers the agent will connect to. In this example, a "stdio" MCP server is configured. This type of server runs as a local process. The Agent starts it using the specified command and args, and then communicates with it via stdin/stdout to discover and execute available tools.

You can find more details about Hugging Face Inference Providers here.

Modern LLMs are built for function calling (or tool use), which enables users to easily build applications tailored to specific use cases and real-world tasks.

A function is defined by its schema, which informs the LLM what it does and what input arguments it expects. The LLM decides when to use a tool, the Agent then orchestrates running the tool and feeding the result back.

InferenceClient implements the same tool calling interface as the OpenAI Chat Completions API, which is the established standard for inference providers and the community.

The MCPClient is the heart of our tool-use functionality. It's now part of huggingface_hub and uses the AsyncInferenceClient to communicate with LLMs.

The full MCPClient code is in here if you want to follow along using the actual code 🤓

​​Here’s a glimpse of how it connects to an MCP server (the add_mcp_server method):

It supports stdio servers for local tools (like accessing your file system), and http servers for remote tools! It's also compatible with sse, which is the previous standard for remote tools.

The MCPClient's process_single_turn_with_tools method is where the LLM interaction happens. It sends the conversation history and available tools to the LLM via AsyncInferenceClient.chat.completions.create(..., stream=True).

First, the method determines all tools the LLM should be aware of for the current turn – this includes tools from MCP servers and any special "exit loop" tools for agent control; then, it makes a streaming call to the LLM:

As chunks arrive from the LLM, the method iterates through them. Each chunk is immediately yielded, then we reconstruct the complete text response and any tool calls.

Once the stream is complete, if the LLM requested any tool calls (now fully reconstructed in final_tool_calls), the method processes each one:

It first checks if the tool called exits the loop (exit_loop_tool). If not, it finds the correct MCP session responsible for that tool and calls session.call_tool(). The result (or error response) is then formatted, added to the conversation history, and yielded so the Agent is aware of the tool's output.

With the MCPClient doing all the job for tool interactions, our Agent class becomes wonderfully simple. It inherits from MCPClient and adds the conversation management logic.

The Agent class is tiny and focuses on the conversational loop, the code can be found here.

When an Agent is created, it takes an agent config (model, provider, which MCP servers to use, system prompt) and initializes the conversation history with the system prompt. The load_tools() method then iterates through the server configurations (defined in agent.json) and calls add_mcp_server (from the parent MCPClient) for each one, populating the agent's toolbox.

The Agent.run() method is an asynchronous generator that processes a single user input. It manages the conversation turns, deciding when the agent's current task is complete.

There are a lot of cool ways to explore and expand upon the MCP Client and the Tiny Agent 🔥 Here are some ideas to get you started:

Pull requests and contributions are welcome! Again, everything here is open source! 💎❤️

#10694. This new chip survives 1300°F (700°C) and could change AI forever

Modern electronics power everything from smartphones to satellites, but they all share a major limitation. Heat. Once temperatures climb above roughly 200 degrees Celsius, most devices begin to break down. For decades, this thermal barrier has been one of the toughest challenges in engineering.

Researchers at the University of Southern California now believe they have found a way past that limit.

In a study published on March 26, 2026 in Science, a team led by Joshua Yang, Arthur B. Freeman Chair Professor at the Ming Hsieh Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering at the USC Viterbi School of Engineering and the USC School of Advanced Computing, unveiled a new type of memory device that continues to operate at 700 degrees Celsius (~1300 degrees Fahrenheit). That temperature exceeds molten lava and goes far beyond anything previously achieved for this class of technology. The device showed no sign of failure. In fact, 700 degrees was simply the maximum their equipment could test.

"You may call it a revolution," Yang said. "It is the best high-temperature memory ever demonstrated."

The new device is known as a memristor, a nanoscale component that can both store data and perform computations. It is constructed like a microscopic layered structure, with two electrodes on either side and a thin ceramic layer in between.

Jian Zhao, the study's first author, built the device using tungsten for the top electrode, hafnium oxide ceramic in the middle, and graphene for the bottom layer. Tungsten has the highest melting point of any element, while graphene, a single-atom-thick sheet of carbon, is known for its exceptional strength and heat resistance.

This combination produced remarkable performance. The device retained data for more than 50 hours at 700 degrees without needing to be refreshed. It also endured over one billion switching cycles at that temperature and operated at just 1.5 volts with speeds measured in tens of nanoseconds.

The discovery was not part of the team's original plan. They were initially attempting to create a different graphene-based device, which did not work as intended. Along the way, they encountered something surprising.

"To be honest, it was by accident, as most discoveries are," Yang said. "If you can predict it, it's usually not surprising, and probably not significant enough."

Further investigation revealed why the device performed so well. In conventional electronics, heat causes metal atoms in the top electrode to slowly migrate through the ceramic layer. Eventually, they reach the bottom electrode, creating a permanent connection that short-circuits the device and leaves it stuck in the on state.

Graphene prevents this failure. Its interaction with tungsten is, as Yang described it, similar to oil and water. Tungsten atoms that approach the graphene surface cannot attach to it. Without a stable point to settle, they drift away instead of forming a conductive bridge. This prevents short circuits and preserves the device's function even under extreme heat.

The researchers confirmed this mechanism using advanced electron microscopy, spectroscopy, and quantum-level simulations. By understanding what happens at the atomic interface, they have turned an unexpected result into a principle that could guide future designs. Other materials with similar surface properties could be identified, which may help scale the technology for industrial production.

Electronics capable of operating above 500 degrees Celsius have long been a goal for space exploration. Venus, for example, has a surface temperature around that level, and every lander sent there has failed in part due to extreme heat. Current silicon-based chips cannot survive such conditions.

"We are now above 700 degrees, and we suspect it will go higher," Yang said.

The potential applications go far beyond space missions. Geothermal energy systems require electronics that can function deep underground, where surrounding rock can glow red-hot. Nuclear and fusion systems also expose equipment to intense heat. Even in everyday settings, durability improves significantly. A device rated for 700 degrees would be extremely robust at the roughly 125-degree temperatures often reached inside automotive electronics.

Why It Matters for Artificial Intelligence

In addition to storing data, the device offers a major advantage for artificial intelligence. Many AI systems rely heavily on matrix multiplication, a mathematical operation used in tasks like image recognition and language processing. Traditional computers perform these calculations step by step, consuming large amounts of energy.

Memristors approach the problem differently. By using Ohm's Law, where voltage times conductance equals current, the device performs calculations directly as electricity flows through it. The result is obtained instantly as the measured current.

"Over 92 percent of the computing in AI systems like ChatGPT is nothing but matrix multiplication," Yang said. "This type of device can perform that in the most efficient way, orders of magnitude faster and at lower energy."

Yang and three co-authors of the study (Qiangfei Xia, Miao Hu, and Ning Ge) have already co-founded a company called TetraMem to commercialize memristor-based AI chips at room temperature. Their lab is already using working chips from TetraMem for machine learning tasks. The high-temperature version described in this research could extend those capabilities to environments where traditional electronics cannot operate, allowing devices such as spacecraft or industrial sensors to process data directly on site.

From Lab Prototype to Real-World Technology

Despite the promising results, Yang emphasizes that practical applications are still some distance away. Memory is only one part of a complete computing system. High-temperature logic circuits will also need to be developed and integrated. In addition, the current devices were built manually at very small scales in a laboratory setting, so manufacturing at scale will take time.

"This is the first step," Yang said. "It's still a long way to go. But logically, you can see: now it makes it possible. The missing component has been made."

From a manufacturing perspective, two of the materials used in the device, tungsten and hafnium oxide, are already widely used in semiconductor production. Graphene is newer but is actively being developed by major companies such as TSMC and Samsung, and it has already been produced at wafer scale in research environments.

The work was conducted through the CONCRETE Center, short for Center of Neuromorphic Computing under Extreme Environments, a multi-university Center of Excellence led by USC and supported by the Air Force Office of Scientific Research and the Air Force Research Laboratory. Key experimental work was carried out in collaboration with Dr. Sabyasachi Ganguli's team at the AFRL Materials Lab in Dayton, Ohio, while theoretical analysis involved USC researchers and collaborators at Kumamoto University in Japan.

For Yang, publication in Science reflects more than a single achievement.

"Space exploration has never been so real, so close, and at such a large scale," he said. "This paper represents a critical leap into a much larger, more exciting frontier."

Materials provided by University of Southern California. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#10693. Friendly Fraud Prevention for Developers: What to Log, Block and Automate

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Friendly fraud prevention comes down to three jobs you can do in code: log the right checkout data, block risky payments before they settle, and automate your response when a dispute still lands. Get the first one wrong and you can't win the dispute later, no matter how good your case is.

In this tutorial, we'll build each piece in Node.js in a way that works with any payment service provider (PSP). Your code owns the data and the logic, and a thin adapter talks to Stripe, Adyen, Checkout.com or whoever processes your payments.

Friendly fraud happens when a customer makes a real purchase, then disputes it with their card issuer. They might claim they didn't authorize it, that it never arrived, or that they canceled. Sometimes it's honest confusion. A spouse used the saved card, or the charge showed up under a name they didn't recognize. Sometimes it's a free refund with extra steps.

Either way, the money leaves your account. A dispute (also called a chargeback) reverses the payment, and your processor charges a dispute fee on top. Lose too many, and the card networks put your account into a monitoring program with higher fees.

It's also common. Visa puts friendly fraud at around 20% of fraudulent disputes globally, and up to 30% for high-volume online merchants. Mastercard goes further: it says first-party fraud makes up 75% of the fraud online businesses experience.

So why is this your problem and not finance's? Because the evidence that wins these disputes is created at checkout, by your code. If your app never stored the customer's IP address, device ID or login history, nobody can produce it three months later when the dispute arrives.

Friendly fraud can be stopped at four points, and each one is a different piece of code:

Most guides only cover stages 1 and 4. The rest of this tutorial walks through all four.

Log four things on every order: the customer's IP address, a device ID, their account ID and the shipping address. Those are the data elements Visa's Compelling Evidence 3.0 (CE3.0) rules check when you fight an "unauthorized" fraud dispute.

Here's how CE3.0 works. You win the dispute if you can show two earlier, undisputed purchases on the same card, made 120 to 365 days before the disputed one. All three purchases must share at least two data elements, and one of them must be the IP address or device ID. In plain terms: same card, same person, same device, and they never complained before.

Most PSPs support CE3.0, including Stripe, Adyen, Checkout.com and Airwallex. But none of them can submit data you never captured. And because the window reaches back a full year, you need to keep these logs for at least 13 months (Mastercard's rule, below).

Mastercard has its own version, called First-Party Trust, for disputes filed under reason code 4837 (no cardholder authorization). It asks for one data point from each of three categories: a device factor (IP address, device ID or fingerprint), a delivery factor (shipping address, email or phone) and a different identity factor (such as account login ID or billing address). On the dispute route, Mastercard calls a lookup service that you host, with named fields such as deviceIpAddress, orderDeviceId, orderEmail and userIdName. That service has to answer in about 2.5 seconds on average and search 13 months of sales data.

First-Party Trust is live in the US. Per Mastercard's October 2026 announcement, it reaches Eastern Europe, the Middle East and Africa from October 2026 and the rest of Europe from July 2027. If you sell into Europe, the logging work is due now.

The good news: one evidence table serves both networks. Capture the data once, then keep the eligibility checks for Visa and Mastercard separate.

Start with a table that stores this data per order, separate from your PSP:

Then capture it in your checkout route. If your app sits behind a proxy or CDN, set Express's trust proxy so req.ip returns the customer's address, not your load balancer's:

The psp object is your adapter: one small module per provider that maps its API to the same shape. Swap providers, and this route doesn't change.

For digital products and SaaS, log usage too. Login timestamps, downloads and feature activity prove the customer used what they paid for, which beats "I never received it" claims.

The cheapest dispute is the one that never happens. Three checkout changes do most of the work: 3D Secure on risky payments, a billing descriptor customers recognize, and a few rules that stop obvious abuse.

Use 3D Secure where risk is higher. 3D Secure (3DS) asks the cardholder to confirm the payment with their bank, often through an app prompt. For authenticated payments, liability for fraud disputes generally shifts from you to the card issuer. Every major PSP supports it, and most let you request it per payment instead of forcing it on everyone. Forcing it everywhere adds friction and costs conversions, so trigger it on risk signals.

Make your billing descriptor obvious. The descriptor is the text on the customer's card statement. If it reads PMT*SRV 8812 instead of your product name, expect "I don't recognize this charge" disputes. Use the brand name customers know, and add a support URL or phone number where your PSP allows it. If you sell several products, use a dynamic descriptor that names each one.

Add a risk check before you charge. Most PSPs include a rules engine, but a small check in your own code keeps the logic portable:

Store the signals array with the order. If a dispute arrives later, you'll know whether the payment looked risky at the time, which helps you decide whether to fight it or accept it.

Keep the rules few and specific. A rule that blocks 5% of good customers to stop 1% of bad ones costs more than the disputes it prevents.

Yes, if you ship physical goods. The window between a successful payment and the moment an order ships is the cheapest place to stop friendly fraud: nothing has left the warehouse, so canceling costs you nothing but the sale. Most fraud tools decide at checkout and never look again.

The pattern is a fulfillment gate. Instead of sending every paid order straight to your warehouse or 3PL, route it through a decision step first:

The verify path does two jobs. Legitimate buyers confirm and their order ships. Buyers planning to dispute see that the store is watching, and a confirmed verification becomes evidence if they dispute anyway.

The hard part is screenOrder. Your own data only shows how a customer behaved with you. A buyer who has filed "item not received" disputes at 10 other stores looks brand new on their first order with yours. That's why post-purchase screening works best on shared data across many merchants.

Chargeflow Prevent is one example of this kind of friendly fraud prevention. It scores each order after checkout and before fulfillment, links device, IP, email and payment behavior across a network of 20,000+ merchants, and returns approve, verify or cancel. Today it runs as a Shopify app, with no checkout changes. A public Prevent API isn't available yet, so on other stacks you'd build the gate above with your own rules and data.

Build an order lookup endpoint. When a cardholder taps "I don't recognize this" in their banking app, the issuer can now ask the merchant for order details before a dispute is filed. Visa does this through Verifi Order Insight, and Mastercard through Ethoca Consumer Clarity. Show the customer a receipt with your logo, the items and the delivery date, and many disputes are never filed.

One endpoint can serve both networks, plus Mastercard's First-Party Trust dispute route. Mastercard's published service levels for this kind of lookup are strict:

The tricky part is matching. Issuers often send partial data, so match on whatever arrives: acquirer reference number (ARN), authorization code, date, amount, currency, and card BIN plus last four digits.

On top of lookups, Visa and many PSPs offer rules-based auto-refunds. Verifi's Rapid Dispute Resolution (RDR) and Visa Resolve refund pre-disputes that match rules you set, such as "refund anything under $25". You don't write code for these, but you do pick the thresholds, so treat them like the REFUND_THRESHOLD below.

If you sell subscriptions, many friendly fraud disputes aren't about stolen cards at all. The customer forgot about a renewal, couldn't find the cancel button, or thinks they canceled. Each of these has a code fix.

Here's a daily job that sends renewal reminders and records that each one went out:

That evidenceLog row matters. When a customer later claims they never knew about the renewal, you can show the exact date you told them.

Automate two things: refunding payments that get flagged before they become chargebacks, and building evidence packets for the ones you fight. Both run off webhooks, and both have hard deadlines that humans miss.

Card networks can warn you before a dispute is filed. Visa runs this through Verifi and Mastercard through Ethoca, and many PSPs pass these alerts or their own early fraud warnings to you by webhook. Refunding at this stage costs you the sale, but you skip the dispute fee and the dispute doesn't count against your ratio.

The threshold is a business call. Refunding a $20 order is cheaper than fighting it; a $900 order with strong evidence may be worth contesting.

When a fraud dispute arrives, check whether it qualifies for CE3.0 by looking for two earlier undisputed orders on the same card that share data with the disputed one:

If you get two matches, pass them to your PSP's CE3.0 evidence fields. On Stripe that's evidence.enhanced_evidence.visa_compelling_evidence_3; other PSPs have their own equivalents. Your adapter handles the mapping. If not, fall back to standard evidence: the IP, receipt, usage logs, renewal reminders and terms acceptance you've been logging all along.

Always submit before the deadline your PSP returns with the dispute. A late response is an automatic loss.

The code above covers the basics. A production system also needs evidence templates per reason code, network deadlines per card brand, retries, and win-rate tracking. That maintenance multiplies with every PSP you add.

PSP-native tools only see that PSP's data, so they miss the usage logs, renewal reminders and support threads in your own app. A dedicated platform connects to your PSPs and lets you send that data in.

Here's what the buy path looks like with the Chargeflow API. Chargeflow ingests disputes from connected PSPs (Stripe, PayPal, Adyen, Checkout.com, Braintree and 20+ others), fires a dispute.created webhook, and you enrich the dispute with the evidence you logged:

Chargeflow then builds the response and submits it to the PSP before the deadline. Pre-dispute alerts work the same way: Chargeflow can refund flagged transactions for you, or send alerts.created and alerts.transaction.linked webhooks so your code issues the refund and reports the result to POST /alerts/{id}/outcome.

Using Claude, ChatGPT or Cursor to build this? Chargeflow publishes its whole developer documentation as one machine-readable file, docs.chargeflow.io/llms-full.txt. Point your assistant at it and it can write the webhook handler and field mapping against the real API, not a guess.

Then your merchants get the disputes, and you need to give them a dispute product without building a dispute team. Chargeflow Connect is built for this. It exposes the same prevention, alerts and recovery engine to your platform in a few delivery models:

EaaS is the most developer-friendly entry point. You POST /public/2025-04-01/evidence with a merchant account_id and a dispute, get back an in_progress record, and receive an evidence.ready webhook with the PDF link, typically in about 30 seconds. Store the evidence id, not the URL, because the download link expires after 7 days. You can run it on auto-pilot (Chargeflow generates and submits) or co-pilot (your merchant approves first).

Don't wait for a customer to dispute a charge to find out your evidence pipeline is broken. Most PSPs give you test cards that create disputes on demand.

One more check before launch: confirm your webhook endpoints verify signatures and return 200 fast. PSPs and Chargeflow retry deliveries that fail, and a slow handler can process the same dispute twice.

If you only do one thing this week, start logging IP address and device ID on every order. Everything else builds on that data.

True fraud is when a criminal uses a stolen card. Friendly fraud is when the real cardholder makes a purchase, then disputes it. Prevention differs: true fraud is stopped at checkout with risk checks and 3DS, while friendly fraud is won with evidence after the fact.

Mostly, yes. Both describe a real cardholder disputing a legitimate charge. "Chargeback fraud" usually implies the customer did it on purpose, while friendly fraud also covers honest mistakes, like a forgotten subscription or a family member's purchase. Visa calls it first-party misuse, and Mastercard calls it first-party fraud.

Check the reason code first. For "unauthorized" fraud claims, submit Visa CE3.0 or Mastercard First-Party Trust evidence if the customer qualifies. For "not received" or "canceled" claims, submit delivery proof, usage logs and your cancellation records. For low-value orders, accepting the dispute or refunding on an alert is often cheaper than fighting it.

Partly. 3DS generally shifts liability for fraud disputes to the issuer, so "I didn't authorize this" claims on authenticated payments rarely cost you. It doesn't help with "item not received" or "I canceled" disputes, which need delivery proof and cancellation records.

No. CE3.0 needs two undisputed purchases on the same card made 120 to 365 days earlier, so it only protects returning customers. For first-time buyers, rely on 3DS and standard evidence.

Yes. Mastercard's First-Party Trust program covers reason code 4837 disputes. It needs one device, one delivery and one extra identity data point, and Mastercard checks them against the cardholder's past purchases. The same evidence table you build for Visa feeds both.

It depends on the stage. At checkout, your PSP's 3D Secure and rules engine. After payment, post-purchase screening such as Chargeflow Prevent holds risky orders before they ship. Before a chargeback, Verifi Order Insight and Ethoca Consumer Clarity show cardholders the order details, while Verifi and Ethoca alerts (offered by many PSPs and by Chargeflow Alerts) and RDR let you refund early. After a chargeback, Visa CE3.0, Mastercard First-Party Trust and dispute automation tools submit the evidence. For developers, the Chargeflow API covers the alert and dispute stages across PSPs, and Chargeflow Connect does the same for platforms.
