#10657. Featherless AI on Hugging Face Inference Providers 🔥

We're thrilled to share that Featherless AI is now a supported Inference Provider on the Hugging Face Hub! Featherless AI joins our growing ecosystem, enhancing the breadth and capabilities of serverless inference directly on the Hub’s model pages. Inference Providers are also seamlessly integrated into our client SDKs (for both JS and Python), making it super easy to use a wide variety of models with your preferred providers.

Featherless AI supports a wide variety of text and conversational models, including the latest open-source models from DeepSeek, Meta, Google, Qwen, and much more.

Featherless AI is a serverless AI inference provider with unique model loading and GPU orchestration abilities that makes an exceptionally large catalog of models available for users. Providers often offer either a low cost of access to a limited set of models, or an unlimited range of models with users managing servers and the associated costs of operation. Featherless provides the best of both worlds offering unmatched model range and variety but with serverless pricing. Find the full list of supported models on the models page.

We're super excited to see what you'll build with this new provider!

Read more about how to use Featherless as an Inference Provider in its dedicated documentation page.

Install or upgrade huggingface_hub to ensure you have version v0.33.0 or better: pip install --upgrade huggingface-hub

For direct requests, i.e. when you use the key from an inference provider, you are billed by the corresponding provider. For instance, if you use a Featherless AI API key you're billed on your Featherless AI account.

For routed requests, i.e. when you authenticate via the Hugging Face Hub, you'll only pay the standard provider API rates. There's no additional markup from us, we just pass through the provider costs directly. (In the future, we may establish revenue-sharing agreements with our provider partners.)

#10656. Among Us player & his mom reveal how they helped save kidnapped girl he met in-game

A 16-year-old boy has revealed how a chance encounter in Among Us led to him and his mother helping rescue a teenage girl who had allegedly been held captive for more than 500 days.

Earlier in November, 17-year-old Kylie Arellano was rescued after secretly asking another player for help while playing Innersloth’s popular social deduction game.

Arellano had been missing since May 2025, when she disappeared from her home in Utah at the age of 15. She was allegedly held against her will in the basement of a home in Huntington, Oregon.

For Colorado teenager Landon Tresp, what began as an ordinary gaming session on October 15 would end with him helping a girl hundreds of miles away escape her alleged captor.

After meeting in Among Us, Landon and Arellano struck up a friendship and began communicating through Discord.

Over the following two weeks, Arellano began opening up about her situation, eventually sending Landon news articles covering her disappearance.

Realizing something was seriously wrong, Landon turned to his mother, Khristina, for help on Halloween. Neither knew that within 24 hours, the girl would finally be free.

Khristina began speaking with Arellano through Discord, but locating the teenager proved challenging as she didn’t know the address where she was being held.

“I knew I had to do everything I could to make sure she was brought to safety and had a second chance,” Khristina recalled.

Determined to find her, Khristina searched online property records before turning to real estate website Zillow. After being sent photos of two potential houses, Arellano recognized the second property.

Teenage girl held captive for 500 days rescued after secretly asking for help in Among Us

Among Us hackers targeted as InnerSloth rush out emergency hotfix

World of Warcraft account helps police locate missing 16-year-old

Khristina contacted the girl’s family and began working with the FBI to bring her home.

Speaking with KOAA, Khristina described how devastating it was to learn just how long Arellano had been missing.

“Just heartbreaking to think that she had been going through what she had for over 520 days and without anyone that she could reach a hand out to and not knowing where you’re at,” she said.

On November 1, authorities arrived at the Oregon residence. Khristina stayed on a video call with Arellano, encouraging her to make the final few steps toward freedom.

“I was on the video chat with her when I told her to face those basement stairs and run up them and down that hallway,” Khristina recalled. “And grab that front door because that was her freedom.”

After more than 500 days away from home, Arellano was finally in the care of law enforcement and was taken for medical treatment and evaluation.

For Landon, seeing the friend he had met just weeks earlier finally reach safety was an overwhelming moment.

“Oh my God, just pure bliss. I was so happy she was safe in that car. I was so happy she was out of that horrible monster’s house,” he said.

Adam Hunter Harmel, 39, has since been indicted on a federal charge of transportation with intent to engage in criminal sexual activity. Prosecutors allege he met the girl online before traveling to Utah and taking her across state lines.

Despite everything that happened, Landon and Arellano haven’t stopped playing video games together.

The pair remain friends, while Khristina continues to speak with Arellano every day. The family is also hoping to meet her in person.

What began with two strangers meeting in Among Us has become a friendship that extends far beyond the game, with Landon and his mother giving Arellano the help she had desperately needed for more than a year.

#10655. Why Transactional Emails Fail After Deployment: A Practical Debugging Guide for Developers

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Transactional emails are easy to overlook during application development. A registration form works, the database stores the user's information, and the backend successfully triggers an email. Everything appears to be functioning as expected.

Then a user reports that their password-reset message never arrived.

The problem might not be in the email template or the sending function. It could involve DNS configuration, authentication failures, message formatting, queue processing, recipient-server policies, or an incorrectly configured production environment.

For developers building SaaS applications, ecommerce platforms, and web services, reliable email delivery is an important part of the user experience. An account-verification message that never arrives can prevent someone from accessing an application, while a delayed security notification can create unnecessary confusion.

Understanding how to investigate these problems requires looking beyond the email-sending function. This guide explores a practical debugging workflow, the technical layers involved, and the tools developers can use to identify common email delivery failures.

One of the first mistakes developers make when troubleshooting email is assuming that a successful API response means the message has reached the recipient.

When an application submits an email through an SMTP server or an email service provider's API, the provider may accept the request and return a successful response. However, the receiving mail server still needs to process the message.

Depending on its configuration and policies, the receiving server might:

Accept the message and place it in the inbox.

Accept the message but classify it as spam.

Reject the message because of authentication or policy issues.

Accept the message but place it in another folder.

A successful request therefore confirms only that a particular stage of the process completed.

Developers should distinguish between three important states:

Submission: The application successfully handed the message to its sending provider.

Acceptance: The receiving mail server accepted responsibility for the message.

Inbox placement: The message became visible in the recipient's expected inbox.

These distinctions make troubleshooting considerably easier. Instead of immediately rewriting an email template, developers can identify which stage is actually failing.

Before investigating external email infrastructure, examine the application's own implementation.

A common example is a password-reset workflow. The application receives a request, generates a temporary token, creates a reset URL, and sends an email containing that URL.

Several problems can occur before the message even reaches an email provider.

The application generates an expired token.

The reset URL points to a staging environment.

An asynchronous task fails before processing the message.

The email service credentials are incorrect.

An API request times out without being retried.

The application records success before confirming the provider's response.

Start by logging the important stages of the process.

For example, a Node.js application might use structured logging:

This example assumes that the email provider returns a message identifier. Adapt the response fields to the actual SDK being used.

Notice that the logs identify the recipient through an internal ID rather than exposing their complete email address.

Avoid logging passwords, authentication tokens, reset URLs, or other sensitive information.

The objective is to establish a traceable record of what happened without introducing additional security risks.

Email authentication is another important area to investigate when messages are rejected or consistently classified as spam.

Three commonly used mechanisms help receiving servers evaluate whether a message is authorized to represent a particular domain.

Sender Policy Framework (SPF) allows a domain owner to specify which servers are authorized to send messages using that domain.

This information is published through DNS.

A simplified SPF record might look like this:

The actual record must reflect the sending services authorized by the domain owner.

Forgetting to authorize a new email provider.

Publishing multiple SPF records for the same domain.

Leaving outdated sending services in the record.

Remember that SPF evaluates the sending infrastructure against the envelope sender domain. It does not automatically guarantee that the visible From address is aligned.

DomainKeys Identified Mail (DKIM) adds a cryptographic signature to outgoing messages.

The receiving server can retrieve the corresponding public key through DNS and verify that the signature is valid.

A mismatch between the configured selector and published record.

Developers integrating multiple email providers should verify that each provider has the correct signing configuration.

Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting, and Conformance (DMARC) builds on SPF and DKIM.

It allows domain owners to define how receiving servers should handle messages that fail authentication and alignment requirements.

A basic monitoring-oriented DMARC record might look like this:

This is an illustrative configuration. The reporting address must be valid, and the domain should have an appropriate monitoring and policy-enforcement plan.

Developers can use MXToolbox to inspect DNS records and investigate common authentication problems.

For additional technical background, SitePoint's guide to HTML email development explains why email environments require different implementation considerations from ordinary web pages.

An email template that looks perfect in a browser can behave differently when rendered by Gmail, Outlook, Apple Mail, or another email client.

This happens because email clients do not implement HTML and CSS in exactly the same way.

A layout may break because of unsupported CSS properties, image restrictions, unexpected font rendering, or differences in how tables are handled.

For this reason, email testing should be part of the development process rather than something performed only after users report a problem.

HTML validation: Check the markup for malformed elements, missing attributes, and unnecessary code.

Rendering tests: Preview the email across desktop and mobile email clients.

Link verification: Confirm that buttons, links, and personalized URLs point to the correct destinations.

Image testing: Check whether the message remains understandable when images are blocked.

Content inspection: Review subject lines, sender information, and the plain-text alternative.

Deliverability checks: Examine authentication, content-related warnings, and potential inbox placement problems.

Developers can also incorporate pre-send diagnostics into their release workflow to identify potential deliverability problems before a message is sent to a larger audience.

The important point is to treat these checks as one part of quality assurance, not as a guarantee that every message will reach the primary inbox.

For more information about email rendering differences, SitePoint's article on essential HTML email coding tips provides useful examples of client-specific behavior.

Testing transactional emails with real customer addresses during development can create unnecessary problems.

A better approach is to use a dedicated testing environment that captures outgoing messages without delivering them to actual recipients.

For example, Mailpit provides a local SMTP server and web interface for inspecting messages during development.

The final output generated by the application.

Another option is Mailtrap, which provides email testing capabilities for development workflows.

Consider a registration feature that sends a welcome message whenever a new user creates an account.

Instead of sending hundreds of test messages to real addresses, developers can configure the development environment to capture them in a testing inbox.

This makes it possible to repeatedly test different templates without affecting actual customers or generating unnecessary email traffic.

A separate testing environment also reduces the risk of accidentally sending development notifications to production users.

Applications that send large numbers of emails often use background workers instead of processing every message during the original HTTP request.

This approach helps keep the application responsive, but it introduces another potential source of failures.

Imagine an ecommerce application that sends order confirmations after checkout.

The application creates an order successfully and places an email task in a queue. However, the background worker becomes unavailable before processing the task.

The customer receives an order confirmation much later than expected, or perhaps not at all.

To investigate these problems, developers should monitor:

Retries are particularly important, but they need to be implemented carefully.

A temporary network failure may justify another attempt. A permanent rejection caused by an invalid recipient address usually does not.

Exponential backoff can help prevent repeated requests from overwhelming an unavailable service.

In a production system, add random jitter to avoid having multiple workers retry simultaneously.

Also consider idempotency. If a worker processes the same task twice, the application should avoid sending duplicate transactional messages whenever possible.

A reliable queue architecture should distinguish between temporary failures and permanent failures rather than retrying every error indefinitely.

Testing before deployment is important, but it cannot reveal every issue that may occur in production.

Real email traffic introduces changing conditions, including recipient-server behavior, sender reputation, invalid addresses, and differences between email providers.

Developers should therefore establish ongoing monitoring.

For Gmail-related monitoring, Google Postmaster Tools provides information about domain reputation, spam rates, and authentication.

It is particularly useful for teams sending enough email to generate meaningful reporting data.

Another useful resource is Can I Email, which documents HTML and CSS feature support across email clients.

These tools address different problems. Monitoring sender reputation will not fix a broken password-reset URL, just as validating HTML will not resolve a DNS authentication failure.

The best approach is to monitor each layer independently.

A repeatable checklist helps developers investigate problems without overlooking important details.

Before releasing a new email feature, review the following:

Confirm that the application successfully submits the message.

Verify that provider credentials and environment variables are correct.

Inspect SPF, DKIM, and DMARC configuration.

Validate the HTML and plain-text versions.

Preview the message on desktop and mobile email clients.

Verify that development and production configurations are separated.

Check delivery events and provider error reports.

Monitor bounce and complaint rates after deployment.

Not every application needs an expensive testing platform or a complicated monitoring stack.

A small project might only require a local email testing environment, basic DNS checks, and structured application logs.

A larger SaaS platform may benefit from automated integration tests, provider webhooks, queue monitoring, authentication reports, and dedicated deliverability testing.

The right setup depends on the application's sending volume, complexity, and the importance of its email workflows.

Reliable email delivery requires more than calling an SMTP function or integrating an email API.

Developers need to understand the complete process, from application logic and message construction to authentication, queue processing, recipient-server acceptance, and inbox placement.

The most effective troubleshooting strategy is to isolate these layers instead of treating every missing message as a template problem.

Start with application logs, inspect provider responses, validate authentication records, test email rendering, and monitor production behavior.

By incorporating these checks into development and deployment workflows, teams can reduce avoidable failures and build applications that communicate more reliably with their users.

Instead of manually managing complex dependencies, wrestling with compilation flags, or building libraries like Triton or CUTLASS from source, you can use the kernels library to instantly fetch and run pre-compiled, optimized kernels.

Spend more time building great models and less time fighting build systems!

#10653. New quantum algorithm solves “impossible” materials problem in seconds

Quantum computers and other advanced quantum technologies rely on specialized quantum materials that behave in unusual ways under the right conditions. In some cases, scientists can even create entirely new quantum properties by carefully changing a material's structure. One striking example involves stacking sheets of graphene and twisting them into a moiré pattern, which can suddenly turn the material into a superconductor.

Researchers can arrange these layers into even more complicated structures, including quasicrystals and super-moiré materials. But predicting how these exotic materials will behave is extraordinarily difficult. Quasicrystals are so mathematically complex that simulating them can involve more than a quadrillion numbers, a scale far beyond the reach of today's most powerful supercomputers.

Quantum Algorithm Solves Massive Materials Problem

Scientists at Aalto University's Department of Applied Physics have now developed a quantum-inspired algorithm capable of handling these enormous non-periodic quantum materials almost instantly. Assistant Professor Jose Lado says the work also highlights a promising feedback cycle within quantum technology itself.

"Crucially, these new quantum algorithms can enable the development of new quantum materials to build new paradigms of quantum computers, creating a productive two-way feedback loop between quantum materials and quantum computers," he explains.

The advance could eventually support the development of dissipationless electronics, which conduct electricity without energy loss. Such systems may help reduce the growing heat and energy demands of AI-driven data centers.

The research team was led by Lado and included doctoral researcher Tiago Antão, who served as the paper's main author; QDOC doctoral researcher Yitao Sun; and Academy Research Fellow Adolfo Fumega. Their findings were recently published in Physical Review Letters as an Editor's Suggestion.

The researchers focused on topological quasicrystals, unusual materials that host unconventional quantum excitations. These excitations are especially valuable because they help protect electrical conductivity from disruptive noise and interference. However, they are distributed unevenly throughout the already highly complex structure of a quasicrystal.

Rather than attempting to directly calculate the full structure of the material, the team reformulated the challenge using methods similar to those used by quantum computers.

"Quantum computers work in exponentially large computational spaces, so we used a special family of algorithms to encode those spaces, known as tensor networks, to compute a quasicrystal with over 268 million sites. Our algorithm shows how colossal problems in quantum materials can be directly solved with the exponential speed-up that comes from encoding the problem as a quantum many-body system," Antão says.

At this stage, the work remains theoretical and was carried out through simulations, but researchers say experimental testing and future applications are already coming into view.

"The quantum-inspired algorithm we demonstrated enables us to create super-moiré quasicrystals several orders of magnitude above the capabilities of conventional methods. That is an instrumental step towards designing topological qubits with super-moiré materials for use in quantum computers, for example," Lado says.

Toward Practical Quantum Computing Applications

According to Lado, the algorithm could eventually be adapted to operate on actual quantum computers once the hardware becomes sufficiently advanced.

"Our method can be adapted to run on real quantum computers, once they reach necessary scale and fidelity. In particular, the new AaltoQ20 and the Finnish Quantum Computing Infrastructure can play a significant role for future demonstrations," Lado says.

The findings suggest that studying and designing exotic quantum materials may become one of the earliest practical applications for quantum algorithms and quantum computing systems.

The project also brings together two major areas of Finnish quantum research: quantum materials and quantum algorithms. It is part of Lado's ERC Consolidator grant ULTRATWISTROICS, which focuses on designing topological qubits using van der Waals materials, as well as the Center of Excellence in Quantum Materials QMAT, whose goal is to advance the quantum technologies of the future.

#10652. Over $60k raised for famous station cat after he suddenly falls ill

Over $60,000 has been raised to help cover the vet bills of a beloved railway station cat in England after he suddenly fell ill.

On November 23, a 12-year-old ginger cat known for greeting passengers at a train station in the UK was taken to the vet after his family noticed he was eating less and sleeping more than usual.

While George’s family is still waiting to find out what made their beloved pet unwell, feline fans from across the globe have shown their support by raising thousands of dollars to help with his treatment.

“George has brought so much happiness, laughter and comfort to so many people over the years, and now we’re doing everything we can to get him back to his happy, healthy self,” reads a post on the station cat’s Facebook page.

“We know times are difficult for so many, and your kind messages, love and good wishes mean more than you could possibly imagine…Thank you for loving our gorgeous ginger boy as much as we do. We’re keeping everything crossed for him.”

In a post shared on George’s GoFundMe page, his family revealed that the cat’s medical bill has already reached $1,958 (£1,500), and mentioned that further investigations into the cat’s health could lead to further costs.

However, since posting the campaign, George has received an outpouring of donations to help cover the costs. As of November 25, the cute cat has raised $60,582 (£46,393) of his $78,000 (£60,000) goal, much to the shock of his owners.

“We are completely overwhelmed and incredibly humbled by the love, kindness and generosity that has been shown towards our little ginger boy,” said George’s social media manager Simone Carter.

#10651. How Long Prompts Block Other Requests - Optimizing LLM Performance

In the previous part of our series on LLM performance, we looked into the differences between the prefill and decode phases during token generation. In short: for the first output token (prefill step), the entire prompt needs to be processed, which can be parallelized efficiently and can saturate GPU utilization. For all later output tokens (decode steps), only a single additional token needs to be processed, which is less compute-intensive but must be done sequentially. When many requests are processed concurrently, any strategy that aims for low latency needs to run prefill steps for newly arriving requests while the decode steps of previously scheduled requests are still ongoing. Concurrent processing of new as well as running requests therefore requires careful balancing between the prefill and decode stages, which presents two major challenges, which we will discuss in the following. One is a readily solvable issue, while the other one constitutes a more fundamental flaw.

Since individual decode steps are not compute-intensive, one can increase throughput by batching decodes of multiple requests. For prefill, however, this approach does not work. Because of the parallelized processing of all prompt tokens, a single prefill step can already saturate GPU utilization. Consequently, in the default chunked-prefill strategy of vLLM, each prefill chunk contains only prompt tokens of a single request. The next request in line has to wait until the previous prefill phase has been finished before its own prefill phase can start.

This sequential scheduling of prefill chunks for different requests poses a challenge: whenever a request with a very long prompt is scheduled for prefill, any subsequent request has to wait for the duration of the long prefill before its processing starts; a long prompt blocks the prefill-queue. (Note that the sequential processing of prefills is the default characteristic of chunked-prefill and only appears when there already is a concurrent request in its decode phase; hence the name "partial prefill".)

Unfortunately, this challenge can neither be solved with vLLM-side priority scheduling (see the first article of this series) nor with a more sophisticated upstream scheduler. The reason is that the long prompt can be scheduled before any subsequent requests exist, so there is nothing the scheduler could wait for.

A straightforward solution would be to process prefill chunks of different requests in parallel. This might not be resource-optimized, as single-request prefill chunks could already saturate compute-power. Any additional prefill executed in parallel would likely prolong the prefill duration a bit and slow down any concurrent decode-requests even further. This would be acceptable if it reduced the latency of short requests and made the system appear more responsive. This approach fails, however, when the next request in line has a long prompt too. In such a case, two compute-intensive prefills would be batched together and result in a severe slowdown.

In one of the latest vLLM updates, an improved strategy has been implemented: it allows for parallel prefills of different requests but with a limit to the number of concurrently processed long prompt requests. An example configuration could enable batching of prefills for four requests, but only one of them may be longer than 10,000 prompt tokens. With such a configuration, the behavior for longer requests is still the same as before: long prompts are processed sequentially. Short requests, however, no longer need to wait for the long prefill of a previous request to finish; short prompts can take a fast lane. These requests no longer suffer from long waiting times and show much lower time-to-first-token metrics.

Of course, parallel prefills can only reduce waiting times; but the time-per-output-token remains elevated during the concurrent long-prefill operation. In this regard, request-parallel prefills show the same behavior and performance as standard chunked-prefill, just with a shorter time-to-first-token.

Whenever prefill and decode of different requests are executed in the same GPU operation, it takes longer than for an isolated decode step. The user experiences an interruption or a slowing down of the token generation by a subsequent request. In particular, a single request with a long prompt is sufficient to slow down all previously scheduled requests that are already in their decode phases.

This is a fundamental flaw in the concurrent processing of prefill and decode on the same GPUs, because there is little you can do:

The difference between ideal concurrent processing (which would be no different from isolated requests), actual concurrent processing, and a disaggregated prefill strategy is shown by the following measurements:

Separating prefill and decode eliminates the slowing-down of token generation in presence of other requests to a large extent, which makes it a very attractive strategy. It comes at the price of a second full-size vLLM deployment (e.g. for Llama-3.3-70B, you would need four H100 GPUs for a prefill worker and another four H100 GPUs for a decode worker if you wanted to support a maximum context length of 130k tokens). Another disadvantage is the uneven GPU utilization: because prefill is compute-intensive but decode is not, the prefill worker will likely saturate GPU utilization before the decode worker does. On the other hand, large clusters could consist of different numbers of prefill and decode workers (depending on load patterns), in order to optimize resource utilization.

Disaggregated prefill is not intended to increase total throughput, rather total "goodput" (i.e. the rate of requests that satisfy latency targets). Consequently, it is not the best use of GPU resources if your application is not sensitive to latency of individual requests.

Another caveat: the disaggregated prefill feature in vLLM is still experimental, and some optimizations and features are not accessible yet. For example, there are currently lower limits on context length, and the decode worker doesn't use CUDA graphs consistently, causing the slower decode of the long-prompt request in the figure above. Fortunately, these are not fundamental obstacles and are likely going to be solved in future versions of vLLM.

#10649. What Actually Happens When a Kafka Region Fails?

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Most Kafka deployments in the industry plan to survive the loss of a single Kafka broker or an availability zone. But that's not enough for critical Tier-0 infrastructure where downtime or data loss of even a few seconds could have a massive business impact.

In such scenarios, the failure model should consider not just the loss of a broker or a zone, but the loss of an entire region. The business is expected to operate without interruption even when a whole region goes down, and it should be possible to also roll the cluster safely while operating in that state, to apply any break-glass changes.

But what actually happens inside Kafka when an entire region goes down? What happens to the replicas, producer writes, and KRaft quorum? And what happens when that region comes back?

Let's walk through these scenarios using a Tier-0 multi-region Kafka architecture.

For a Tier-0 multi-region Kafka cluster, we need three different regions with isolated failure domains and a minimum of two brokers in each region.

Brokers in each region should be configured with rack awareness to indicate their failure domains as follows:

For Tier-0 workloads, each topic's partitions should be configured to have a replication factor (RF) of 6. Kafka's rack-aware replica assignment will spread the replicas across the three regions. If the automatic replica assignment doesn't allocate two replicas per region, we have to explicitly reassign replicas immediately after topic creation to meet our availability guarantees.

This way, if one region goes down entirely, we still have four replicas surviving and the cluster would still continue to operate.

But just running brokers in multiple regions is not the solution here. In fact, that's the easy part. The hard question is, what guarantee remains when one of those regions disappears, and does it solve the business needs?

The two brokers in that region become unavailable, leaving four surviving replicas across Regions B and C.

For any partitions whose leaders were in Region A, Kafka needs to elect new leaders from the surviving in-sync replicas.

But having four surviving replicas alone does not determine whether Kafka will continue accepting writes.

The next step is to define what is considered a successful write in this Kafka setup. For this, we need two configs:

min.insync.replicas determines the minimum number of replicas that should be present in the in-sync replica set (ISR) of a partition for Kafka to accept writes when producers use acks=all.

acks=all is a producer-side config that ensures that the producer will get an acknowledgment only when the write has been successfully replicated to the required in-sync replicas.

These two settings work together to satisfy the durability guarantees we want.

When all three regions are healthy, ISR would include all six replicas. Let's say one region goes down, then the ISR would drop down to four.

Since minISR is three, writes will still continue to work.

There may be temporary interruptions while Kafka detects the failure, elects new leaders, and clients reconnect to them. But once the surviving leaders are available, the cluster can continue accepting writes as long as the ISR requirements are met.

The goal isn't availability at any cost, but rather the system should be available as long as the durability guarantees that we designed for can be maintained.

Now let's make the scenario more interesting.

Region A is still down. We have four replicas surviving across Regions B and C.

What if we need to roll the cluster one broker at a time, to apply any break-glass changes?

During that time, the ISR can go down from four to three. But since minISR is three, writes will still continue to work.

Let's look at how the cluster behaves under different failure scenarios.

Kafka will stop accepting writes only when the surviving ISR drops below three.

This is an important distinction for Tier-0 workloads.

It's not sufficient to design a cluster that survives a region failure. We also need to consider whether the cluster can continue operating safely while already in that degraded state.

So far, we focused on the data plane. Now switching gears, the KRaft controllers have a completely different availability model.

They form the metadata quorum, and a majority is needed to continue operation.

For our setup, five controllers could be distributed as 2 + 2 + 1 across the three regions, requiring a majority of three to maintain quorum.

If either of the regions containing two controllers goes down, three controllers remain. If the region containing one controller goes down, four remain.

So, the controller quorum survives the loss of any one region.

But, unlike brokers, we cannot necessarily roll the controllers at that point because taking one controller down could cause the quorum to drop below three.

With a static quorum, one way to solve this is to use more controllers, and a 3 + 3 + 3 distribution would provide this. Losing one region would leave six controllers with room to still roll the controllers, as we only need five to maintain quorum.

On the flip side, an increase in quorum size also increases the coordination overhead. The official Kafka documentation typically recommends three or five controllers, which tolerate one or two concurrent failures respectively.

Alternatively, with dynamic KRaft quorum (KIP-853), introduced in Kafka 3.9, we can add or remove controllers from the voting quorum without restarting the cluster.

For example, with our 2 + 2 + 1 setup, if a region containing two controllers goes down, the remaining three controllers can still maintain quorum. We can then remove the failed controllers from the voting membership, one at a time, reducing the quorum size to three. This allows us to roll one of the surviving controllers while still maintaining the new majority of two.

However, dynamic quorum reconfiguration is not automatic. The surviving controllers must be able to maintain quorum and successfully commit the membership changes before we can proceed with the controller restart.

You need to consider whether you want the same availability guarantee for the controllers as that of the data plane, and whether dynamic quorum reconfiguration during a regional outage is acceptable for your Tier-0 workloads.

So far, we assumed that a region either works or goes down completely.

But the WAN itself becomes a failure mode.

In this setup, a partly working WAN between two regions can be more dangerous than a link that's completely down.

Increased latency, packet loss, or intermittent connectivity issues between regions can cause replication to lag, ultimately resulting in replicas falling out of ISR.

The three regions might be independently healthy, but if the connectivity between them is not, then the availability of the cluster might be impacted.

Going back to the CAP theorem, to tolerate a network partition, we must choose between consistency and availability.

So, if a partition's ISR falls below the configured min.insync.replicas of three due to a network partition, Kafka stops accepting writes with acks=all rather than weakening those guarantees.

Similarly, if the KRaft controller quorum is lost, then no metadata changes, like leader elections, can happen in the cluster, even though existing data-plane traffic may continue for some time.

The availability guarantees we discussed also come with their own costs.

The first cost is client latency. With cross-region replication and acks=all, the network latency between these regions directly affects producer latency. Consumers can also pay the WAN latency cost when consuming from partition leaders located in a different region.

The second cost is replication overhead. With RF=6, there is additional storage, network traffic, and replication-related coordination cost in the brokers compared to a smaller number of replicas.

So, in an architecture like this, monitoring the health of the network paths between these regions is as critical as monitoring the Kafka brokers and controllers.

Metrics like round-trip latency (RTT) between regions, packet loss, TCP retransmissions, connection errors/timeouts, and network throughput/bandwidth utilization are a good start.

When one region goes down, all the partition leaders in that region would move to the two other surviving regions.

This implies that those two regions would have to handle more producer and consumer traffic, network throughput, and disk I/O.

Even if the cluster is designed to satisfy its ISR and controller quorum requirements, if it's not sized to handle these failures when one region goes down, the surviving regions would be overloaded, resulting in higher latencies, timeouts, and operational instability.

So, for Tier-0 infrastructure, capacity planning should always be done for failure states and not stop at normal operations.

Now let's say Region A comes back online.

The brokers in the recovered region might have to catch up on a significant amount of data before they become fully in sync again.

This can result in a sudden burst of cross-region network traffic and disk I/O across all regions.

Region recovery needs to be controlled so that it doesn't overwhelm the healthy part of the cluster.

This can be achieved by throttling the replica catch-up, with the trade-off of longer recovery time to minimize the impact on live production traffic.

Replication throttling needs a deeper discussion of its own, so we won't go into details here.

The important point is that bringing a failed region back online is not simply a matter of restarting its brokers. We need to make sure that the recovery process itself doesn't impact the business.

Before putting a Tier-0 multi-region Kafka cluster into production, validate these scenarios:

There is no shortage of ways to deploy Kafka across multiple regions. The challenge here is to pick the right architecture that addresses all our durability guarantees.

For Tier-0 workloads, this means designing the architecture around failures first.

What happens when a region goes down? Can we still roll the cluster? What continues to work, and at what point do we deliberately stop accepting writes?

Lastly, can we safely bring back the region that was down without impacting the business?

That is ultimately the difference between simply running Kafka across multiple regions versus actually supporting a mission-critical Tier-0 workload.

#10648. NASA’s new AI space chip could let spacecraft think for themselves

NASA is developing a powerful new computer chip designed to dramatically increase the intelligence and performance of future spacecraft. Through a commercial partnership, the project is creating advanced processing technology capable of helping spacecraft operate more independently during missions far from Earth.

NASA's High Performance Spaceflight Computing project is focused on boosting the computing capabilities of spacecraft used in space exploration. Current missions rely on older processors because they are durable enough to survive the extreme conditions of space. While those chips are dependable, they lack the performance needed for more advanced missions.

The agency says newer and far more capable processors are essential for future autonomous spacecraft, faster onboard scientific analysis, and supporting astronauts during missions to the Moon and Mars.

"Building on the legacy of previous space processors, this new multicore system is fault-tolerant, flexible, and extremely high-performing," said Eugene Schwanbeck, program element manager in NASA's Game Changing Development program at the agency's Langley Research Center, in Hampton, Virginia. "NASA's commitment to advancing spaceflight computing is a triumph of technical achievement and collaboration."

Radiation Hardened Processor Faces Extreme Testing

At the center of the project is a new radiation-hardened processor built to deliver up to 100 times the computing power of today's spaceflight computers while surviving the harsh environment of space. Engineers at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) in Southern California are running a wide range of tests designed to simulate those conditions.

"We are putting these new chips through the wringer by carrying out radiation, thermal, and shock tests while also evaluating their performance through a rigorous functional test campaign," said Jim Butler, High Performance Space Computing project manager at JPL.

To qualify for spaceflight, the processor must withstand intense electromagnetic radiation and dramatic temperature fluctuations that can damage electronics. High-energy particles from the Sun and deep space can also trigger computer errors that force spacecraft into "safe mode," temporarily shutting down nonessential systems until engineers resolve the issue.

NASA is also testing how the chip handles the challenges of planetary landings.

"To simulate real-world performance, we are using high-fidelity landing scenarios from real NASA missions that would typically require power-intensive hardware to process huge volumes of landing-sensor data," said Butler. "This is an exciting time for us to be working on hardware that will enable NASA's next giant leaps."

Testing at JPL began in February and is expected to continue for several months. Early results have been highly encouraging. According to NASA, the processor is functioning as intended and has shown performance levels roughly 500 times greater than the radiation-hardened chips currently used in spacecraft.

The team also marked the beginning of testing with a symbolic moment by sending an email titled "Hello Universe," referencing the famous introductory messages used during the early days of computer programming.

AI Powered Spacecraft and Deep Space Missions

The processor is being developed jointly by JPL and Microchip Technology Inc., based in Chandler, Arizona. The company is working with NASA through a commercial partnership, and sample chips have already been shared with defense and commercial aerospace partners.

The technology is expected to play a major role in the future of autonomous spacecraft. With onboard artificial intelligence, spacecraft could respond to unexpected situations in real time when communication delays make human control impractical. The chip could also help deep space missions process, store, and transmit massive amounts of scientific data back to Earth more efficiently.

NASA says the processor may eventually support crewed missions to the Moon and Mars as well.

Small Processor With Massive Computing Power

The device is known as a system-on-a-chip (or SoC), meaning it combines the essential components of a computer into a single compact unit. The processor includes central processing units, computational offloads, advanced networking systems, memory, and input/output interfaces.

SoCs are widely used in smartphones and tablets because they are compact and energy efficient. However, NASA's version is designed to survive for years in deep space, potentially traveling millions (or even billions) of miles from Earth without maintenance or repairs.

Once the processor is certified for use in space, NASA plans to integrate it into a wide variety of missions, including Earth orbiters, planetary rovers, deep space probes, and crewed habitats.

The technology could also have benefits on Earth. Microchip plans to adapt the processor for industries such as aviation and automotive manufacturing.

The project is managed by the Space Technology Mission Directorate's Game Changing Development (GCD) program at NASA Langley. The GCD program and JPL, which is managed by Caltech in Pasadena, California, oversaw the development process from mission planning and industry studies through final delivery.

NASA JPL selected Microchip as a partner in 2022, and the company funded its own research and development work on the processor.

Groq supports a wide variety of text and conversational models, including the latest open-source models such as Meta's Llama 4, Qwen's QWQ-32B, and many more.

At the heart of Groq's technology is the Language Processing Unit (LPU™), a new type of end-to-end processing unit system that provides the fastest inference for computationally intensive applications with a sequential component, such as Large Language Models (LLMs). LPUs are designed to overcome the limitations of GPUs for inference, offering significantly lower latency and higher throughput. This makes them ideal for real-time AI applications.

Groq offers fast AI inference for openly-available models. They provide an API that allows developers to easily integrate these models into their applications. It offers an on-demand, pay-as-you-go model for accessing a wide range of openly-available LLMs.

#10645. Forget electrons, this breakthrough uses light-matter particles to power AI

Eighty years after the creation of ENIAC, the world's first general-purpose electronic computer, researchers at the University of Pennsylvania are exploring a new way to power the future of computing. Instead of relying entirely on electrons, which have formed the backbone of computers since the 1940s, scientists are now turning to light.

ENIAC, developed by Penn researchers J. Presper Eckert and John Mauchly, helped launch the modern computing era by using streams of electrons to solve complex mathematical problems. That same electronic approach still powers today's computers, smartphones, and AI systems. But as artificial intelligence grows more demanding, the limits of electron-based hardware are becoming harder to ignore.

Electrons carry an electrical charge, which creates several challenges inside modern computer chips. As they move through materials, they generate heat and face resistance that wastes energy. Those problems become even more difficult as chips grow more complex and process enormous amounts of data for AI applications.

Researchers led by Penn physicist Bo Zhen in the School of Arts & Sciences believe photons, the particles that make up light, could help solve some of these issues.

"Because they are charge-neutral and have zero rest mass, photons can carry information quickly over long distances with minimal loss, dominating communications technology," explains Li He, co-first author of a paper published in Physical Review Letters and a former postdoctoral researcher in the Zhen Lab. "But that neutrality means they barely interact with their environment, making them bad at the sort of signal-switching logic that computers depend on."

In other words, light is excellent for carrying information quickly and efficiently, but it struggles with the switching operations needed for computing.

Combining Light and Matter for AI Computing

To overcome that problem, Zhen's team developed a special quasiparticle called an exciton-polariton. The particle forms when photons are strongly linked with electrons inside an atomically thin semiconductor material. This combination allows light to interact much more effectively, making it capable of performing the signal switching required for computing tasks.

The breakthrough could be especially important for artificial intelligence systems, which consume enormous amounts of power.

Many experimental photonic AI chips already use light to handle certain calculations at high speed. However, when these systems need to perform nonlinear activation steps, such as decision-making operations, they usually must convert light signals back into electronic ones. That conversion slows the process and increases energy use, reducing the benefits of photonic computing.

Using exciton-polaritons, the Penn researchers demonstrated all-light switching while using only about 4 quadrillionths of a joule of energy. That amount is extraordinarily small, far below the energy needed to briefly power a tiny LED light.

Toward Faster and More Efficient AI Chips

If the technology can be successfully scaled, it could lead to photonic chips capable of processing information directly from cameras without repeated conversions between light and electricity. The approach could also lower the massive energy demands of large AI systems and potentially support basic quantum computing functions on future chips.

Bo Zhen is the Jin K. Lee Presidential Associate Professor in the Department of Physics and Astronomy in the School of Arts & Sciences at the University of Pennsylvania.

Li He was a postdoctoral researcher in the Zhen Lab in Penn Arts & Sciences. He is currently an assistant professor at Montana State University.

Additional authors on the study include Zhi Wang and Bumho Kim from the University of Pennsylvania's School of Arts & Sciences.

The research was supported by the US Office of Naval Research (N00014-20-1-2325 and N00014-21-1-2703) and the Sloan Foundation.

#10644. (LoRA) Fine-Tuning FLUX.1-dev on Consumer Hardware

In our previous post, Exploring Quantization Backends in Diffusers, we dived into how various quantization techniques can shrink diffusion models like FLUX.1-dev, making them significantly more accessible for inference without drastically compromising performance. We saw how bitsandbytes, torchao, and others reduce memory footprints for generating images.

Performing inference is cool, but to make these models truly our own, we also need to be able to fine-tune them. Therefore, in this post, we tackle efficient fine-tuning of these models with peak memory use under ~10 GB of VRAM on a single GPU. This post will guide you through fine-tuning FLUX.1-dev using QLoRA with the diffusers library. We'll showcase results from an NVIDIA RTX 4090. We'll also highlight how FP8 training with torchao can further optimize speed on compatible hardware.

We aim to fine-tune black-forest-labs/FLUX.1-dev to adopt the artistic style of Alphonse Mucha, using a small dataset.

The model consists of three main components:

In our QLoRA approach, we focus exclusively on fine-tuning the transformer component. The text encoders and VAE remain frozen throughout training.

We used a diffusers training script (slightly modified from here designed for DreamBooth-style LoRA fine-tuning of FLUX models. Also, a shortened version to reproduce the results in this blogpost (and used in the Google Colab) is available here. Let's examine the crucial parts for QLoRA and memory efficiency:

LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) Deep Dive: LoRA makes model training more efficient by keeping track of the weight updates with low-rank matrices. Instead of updating the full weight matrix W W W, LoRA learns two smaller matrices A A A and B B B. The update to the weights for the model is ΔW=BA \Delta W = B A ΔW=BA, where A∈Rr×k A \in \mathbb{R}^{r \times k} A∈Rr×k and B∈Rd×r B \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times r} B∈Rd×r. The number r r r (called rank) is much smaller than the original dimensions, which means less parameters to update. Lastly, α \alpha α is a scaling factor for the LoRA activations. This affects how much LoRA affects the updates, and is often set to the same value as the r r r or a multiple of it. It helps balance the influence of the pre-trained model and the LoRA adapter. For a general introduction to the concept, check out our previous blog post: Using LoRA for Efficient Stable Diffusion Fine-Tuning.

QLoRA: The Efficiency Powerhouse: QLoRA enhances LoRA by first loading the pre-trained base model in a quantized format (typically 4-bit via bitsandbytes), drastically cutting the base model's memory footprint. It then trains LoRA adapters (usually in FP16/BF16) on top of this quantized base. This dramatically lowers the VRAM needed to hold the base model.

For instance, in the DreamBooth training script for HiDream 4-bit quantization with bitsandbytes reduces the peak memory usage of a LoRA fine-tune from ~60GB down to ~37GB with negligible-to-none quality degradation. The very same principle is what we apply here to fine-tune FLUX.1 on a consumer-grade hardware.

8-bit Optimizer (AdamW): Standard AdamW optimizer maintains first and second moment estimates for each parameter in 32-bit (FP32), which consumes a lot of memory. The 8-bit AdamW uses block-wise quantization to store optimizer states in 8-bit precision, while maintaining training stability. This technique can reduce optimizer memory usage by ~75% compared to standard FP32 AdamW. Enabling it in the script is straightforward:

Gradient Checkpointing: During forward pass, intermediate activations are typically stored for backward pass gradient computation. Gradient checkpointing trades computation for memory by only storing certain checkpoint activations and recomputing others during backpropagation.

Cache Latents: This optimization technique pre-processes all training images through the VAE encoder before the beginning of the training. It stores the resulting latent representations in memory. During the training, instead of encoding images on-the-fly, the cached latents are directly used. This approach offers two main benefits:

Setting up 4-bit Quantization (BitsAndBytesConfig):

This section demonstrates the QLoRA configuration for the base model:

Defining LoRA Configuration (LoraConfig): Adapters are added to the quantized transformer:

Only these LoRA parameters become trainable.

Before we launch the QLoRA fine-tune we can save a huge chunk of VRAM and wall-clock time by caching outputs of text encoders once.

At training time the dataloader simply reads the cached embeddings instead of re-encoding the caption, so the CLIP/T5 encoder never has to sit in GPU memory.

By combining this with cached VAE latents (--cache_latents) you whittle the active model down to just the quantized transformer + LoRA adapters, keeping the whole fine-tune comfortably under 10 GB of GPU memory.

For this demonstration, we leveraged an NVIDIA RTX 4090 (24GB VRAM) to explore its performance. The full training command using accelerate is shown below.

Configuration for RTX 4090: On our RTX 4090, we used a train_batch_size of 1, gradient_accumulation_steps of 4, mixed_precision="bf16", gradient_checkpointing=True, use_8bit_adam=True, a LoRA rank of 4, and resolution of 512x768. Latents were cached with cache_latents=True.

Training Time (RTX 4090): Fine-tuning for 700 steps on the Alphonse Mucha dataset took approximately 41 minutes on the RTX 4090 with train_batch_size of 1 and resolution of 512x768.

Output Quality: The ultimate measure is the generated art. Here are samples from our QLoRA fine-tuned model on the derekl35/alphonse-mucha-style dataset:

This table compares the primary bf16 precision results. The goal of the fine-tuning was to teach the model the distinct style of Alphonse Mucha.

The fine-tuned model nicely captured Mucha's iconic art nouveau style, evident in the decorative motifs and distinct color palette. The QLoRA process maintained excellent fidelity while learning the new style.

The results are nearly identical, showing that QLoRA performs effectively with both fp16 and bf16 mixed precision.

For users with NVIDIA GPUs possessing compute capability 8.9 or greater (such as the H100, RTX 4090), even greater speed efficiencies can be achieved by leveraging FP8 training via the torchao library.

We fine-tuned FLUX.1-dev LoRA on an H100 SXM GPU slightly modifieddiffusers-torchao training scripts. The following command was used:

The training run had a peak memory usage of 36.57 GB and completed in approximately 20 minutes.

Qualitative results from this FP8 fine-tuned model are also available:

Key steps to enable FP8 training with torchao involve:

For a more detailed guide and code snippets, please refer to this gist and the diffusers-torchao repository.

After training your LoRA adapters, you have two main approaches for inference.

One approach is to load your trained LoRA adapters on top of the base model.

For when you want maximum efficiency with a single style, you can merge the LoRA weights into the base model.

While we showcased results on an RTX 4090, the same code can be run on more accessible hardware like the T4 GPU available in Google Colab for free.

On a T4, you can expect the fine-tuning process to take significantly longer around 4 hours for the same number of steps. This is a trade-off for accessibility, but it makes custom fine-tuning possible without high-end hardware. Be mindful of usage limits if running on Colab, as a 4-hour training run might push them.

QLoRA, coupled with the diffusers library, significantly democratizes the ability to customize state-of-the-art models like FLUX.1-dev. As demonstrated on an RTX 4090, efficient fine-tuning is well within reach, yielding high-quality stylistic adaptations. Furthermore, for users with the latest NVIDIA hardware, torchao enables even faster training through FP8 precision.

Sharing your fine-tuned LoRA adapters is a fantastic way to contribute to the open-source community. It allows others to easily try out your styles, build on your work, and helps create a vibrant ecosystem of creative AI tools.

#10643. This website has GTA 6 fans queuing for hours to take over a stranger’s PS5 and play for free

A GTA 6 player has created a website that allows anyone to play Rockstar Games’ latest release for free by remotely taking control of their PS5.

While GTA 6 is currently available on PS5 and Xbox Series X/S, those without either console have been left waiting for Rockstar to bring the game to PC.

However, a website called PlayMyPS5 is giving players another way to experience Vice City without having to purchase the game or a console, while attempting to get the internet to complete its story together.

PlayMyPS5 broadcasts gameplay directly from a physical PS5, allowing visitors to join a public queue and remotely control the console through their web browser.

Each player is given five minutes to play before control is handed over to the next person in line. Players have 20 seconds to claim their turn, while remaining idle for 30 seconds will bring their session to an early end.

The website supports controllers, keyboard and mouse, and mobile touchscreen controls. Players can also watch others explore Vice City and communicate through a live chat while waiting for their turn.

There are no downloads, payments, or registration requirements to join the queue, and players can rejoin once their session ends.

The project was created after its developers realized their PS5 spent much of its time sitting unused. Now, they’re encouraging visitors to work together to complete every GTA 6 story mission.

The creators are also attempting to raise $993 to purchase a second PS5, allowing more people to play simultaneously and reducing queue times. Other PS5 owners with a copy of GTA 6 can volunteer to share their consoles through the platform.

#10642. Scientists are seriously asking if bees and ChatGPT are conscious

You might think a honey bee foraging in your garden and a browser window running ChatGPT have nothing in common. But recent scientific research has been seriously considering the possibility that either, or both, might be conscious.

There are many different ways of studying consciousness. One of the most common is to measure how an animal – or artificial intelligence (AI) – acts.

But two new papers on the possibility of consciousness in animals and AI suggest new theories for how to test this – one that strikes a middle ground between sensationalism and knee-jerk skepticism about whether humans are the only conscious beings on Earth.

Questions around consciousness have long sparked fierce debate.

That’s in part because conscious beings might matter morally in a way that unconscious things don’t. Expanding the sphere of consciousness means expanding our ethical horizons. Even if we can’t be sure something is conscious, we might err on the side of caution by assuming it is – what philosopher Jonathan Birch calls the precautionary principle for sentience.

The recent trend has been one of expansion.

For example, in April 2024 a group of 40 scientists at a conference in New York proposed the New York Declaration on Animal Consciousness. Subsequently signed by over 500 scientists and philosophers, this declaration says consciousness is realistically possible in all vertebrates (including reptiles, amphibians and fishes) as well as many invertebrates, including cephalopods (octopus and squid), crustaceans (crabs and lobsters) and insects.

In parallel with this, the incredible rise of large language models, such as ChatGPT, has raised the serious possibility that machines may be conscious.

Five years ago, a seemingly ironclad test of whether something was conscious was to see if you could have a conversation with it. Philosopher Susan Schneider suggested if we had an AI that convincingly mused on the metaphysics of consciousness, it may well be conscious.

By those standards, today we would be surrounded by conscious machines. Many have gone so far as to apply the precautionary principle here too: the burgeoning field of AI welfare is devoted to figuring out if and when we must care about machines.

Yet all of these arguments depend, in large part, on surface-level behavior. But that behavior can be deceptive. What matters for consciousness is not what you do, but how you do it.

A new paper in Trends in Cognitive Sciences that one of us (Colin Klein) coauthored, drawing on previous work, looks to the machinery rather than the behavior of AI.

It also draws on the cognitive science tradition to identify a plausible list of indicators of consciousness based on the structure of information processing. This means one can draw up a useful list of indicators of consciousness without having to agree on which of the current cognitive theories of consciousness is correct.

Some indicators (such as the need to resolve trade-offs between competing goals in contextually appropriate ways) are shared by many theories. Most other indicators (such as the presence of informational feedback) are only required by one theory but indicative in others.

Importantly, the useful indicators are all structural. They all have to do with how brains and computers process and combine information.

The verdict? No existing AI system (including ChatGPT) is conscious. The appearance of consciousness in large language models is not achieved in a way that is sufficiently similar to us to warrant attribution of conscious states.

Yet at the same time, there is no bar to AI systems – perhaps ones with a very different architecture to today’s systems – becoming conscious.

The lesson? It’s possible for AI to behave as if conscious without being conscious.

Biologists are also turning to mechanisms – how brains work – to recognize consciousness in non-human animals.

In a new paper in Philosophical Transactions B, we propose a neural model for minimal consciousness in insects. This is a model that abstracts away from anatomical detail to focus on the core computations done by simple brains.

Our key insight is to identify the kind of computation our brains perform that gives rise to experience.

This computation solves ancient problems from our evolutionary history that arise from having a mobile, complex body with many senses and conflicting needs.

Importantly, we don’t identify the computation itself – there is science yet to be done. But we show that if you could identify it, you’d have a level playing field to compare humans, invertebrates, and computers.

The problem of consciousness in animals and in computers appear to pull in different directions.

For animals, the question is often how to interpret whether ambiguous behavior (like a crab tending its wounds) indicates consciousness.

For computers, we have to decide whether apparently unambiguous behavior (a chatbot musing with you on the purpose of existence) is a true indicator of consciousness or mere roleplay.

Yet as the fields of neuroscience and AI progress, both are converging on the same lesson: when making judgement about whether something is consciousness, how it works is proving more informative than what it does.

Materials provided by The Conversation. Original written by Colin Klein and Andrew Barron. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#10641. Transformers backend integration in SGLang

Hugging Face transformers library is the standard for working with state-of-the-art models — from experimenting with cutting-edge research to fine-tuning on custom data. Its simplicity, flexibility, and expansive model zoo make it a powerful tool for rapid development.

But once you're ready to move from notebooks to production, inference performance becomes mission-critical. That’s where SGLang comes in.

Designed for high-throughput, low-latency inference, SGLang now offers seamless integration with transformers as a backend. This means you can pair the flexibility of transformers with the raw performance of SGLang.

Let’s dive into what this integration enables and how you can use it.

SGLang now supports Hugging Face transformers as a backend, letting you run any transformers-compatible model with high-performance inference out of the box.

No native support needed — SGLang automatically falls back to Transformers when needed, or you can set impl="transformers" explicitly.

Let’s walk through a simple text generation example with meta-llama/Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct to compare both approaches.

transformers library is great for experimentation, small-scale tasks and training, but it's not optimized for high-volume or low-latency scenarios.

SGLang takes a different track, prioritizing efficiency with features like RadixAttention (a memory-efficient attention mechanism). Inference with SGLang is noticeably faster and more resource-efficient, especially under load. Here’s the same task in SGlang using an offline engine:

Or you can spin a server and send requests:

Note that SGLang also offers an OpenAI-compatible API, making it a drop-in replacement for external services.

With the new transformers backend integration, SGLang can now automatically fall back to using transformers models it doesn’t natively support. This means in practice:

This unlocks faster inference and optimized deployment (e.g enabling RadixAttention) without sacrificing the simplicity and versatility of transformers ecosystem.

Note that specifying the impl parameter is optional. If the model is not natively supported by SGLang, it switches to transformers implementation on its own.

Any model on the Hugging Face Hub that works with transformers using trust_remote_code=True and properly implements attention is compatible with SGLang. You can find the exact requirements in the official documentation. If your custom model meets these criteria, all you need to do is set trust_remote_code=True when loading it.

Kyutai Team’s Helium isn’t yet natively supported by SGLang. This is where transformers backend shines, enabling optimized inference without waiting for native support.

There are several key areas we are actively working on to enhance this integration:

Performance Improvements: transformer models currently lag behind the native integration in terms of performance.Our primary objective is to optimize and narrow this gap.

VLM Integration: we are also working toward adding support for Vision-Language Models (VLM) to broaden the range of capabilities and use cases.

#10640. How to Build an Accessible Gold Value Calculator in Vanilla JavaScript

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Ask anyone selling an old chain or a broken ring what they want to know, and it's one thing: what is this worth? A small calculator can answer that in a second, but most of the ones you find online get the details wrong. They ignore troy ounces, treat 14K as 58.5% one day and 58.3% the next, or show a "value" that no buyer will ever pay.

In this tutorial, we'll build a gold value calculator that gets those details right. It runs on plain HTML and JavaScript, updates as the user types, works with a screen reader, keeps its state in a shareable URL and pulls a live spot price through a small Node.js endpoint. The calculation lives in one pure function, so we can test it in a few lines.

Every gold calculator comes down to three inputs: how much the item weighs, how much of that weight is actually gold, and what pure gold is trading for today.

Purity is measured in karats, out of 24. A 14K ring is 14 parts gold and 10 parts other metals, so it's 14 ÷ 24 = 58.3% gold. You'll also see 14K stamped as "585", which is the hallmark many manufacturers use for the same alloy. For a calculator, the karat fraction is the safer default:

The second detail most tutorials miss is the unit. Gold spot prices are quoted in USD per troy ounce, which is 31.1035 grams, not the 28.35-gram ounce on a kitchen scale. Jewelers also use pennyweight (dwt), which is 1.5552 grams. If your calculator multiplies grams by a per-ounce price without converting, every result is wrong by a factor of 31.

Put together, the formula looks like this:

For example, with gold at $2,400 per troy ounce, 10 grams of 14K gold contains 5.83 grams of pure gold, which is worth $449.85 at melt.

That $449.85 is the value of the gold content alone. Refiners and buyers pay a percentage of it, because refining, assaying and handling cost money. Depending on the buyer, the item and the market, the payout can sit well below melt value.

That gap is why good production tools separate the two numbers. A dedicated scrap jewelry gold calculator, like the one The Alloy Market offers, lets sellers estimate what their gold is worth from its weight and karat before they send anything in. Our calculator does the same job with a payout field: leave it at 100% to see melt value, or enter a buyer's rate to see a realistic offer.

Start with real form controls and a visible

A few choices here matter more than they look:

A little CSS gives touch-friendly controls. Keeping inputs at 16px (1rem) also stops iOS Safari from zooming in when a field gets focus.

The biggest problem with most calculator snippets is that the math is buried inside an event handler, mixed with getElementById calls. You can't test it, and you can't reuse it on a server. Put the calculation and validation in their own module instead:

Both functions take plain values and return plain values. They don't know a DOM exists, which means the same file can run in the browser, in Node.js and in your test runner.

Notice that we don't round inside the calculation. Rounding happens once, at display time. Rounding in the middle of a chain of multiplications is a classic way to end up a few cents off.

Now connect the form to the module. Listening for the input event on the form itself catches changes from every field, including the dropdowns, so there's no need to wire up each control separately.

With the markup, CSS and script in place, here's the finished calculator showing our 10 g, 14K example with an 80% buyer payout:

Asking users to type the spot price works, but prefilling it is friendlier. Don't call a metals price API straight from the browser, though. Your API key would be visible to anyone who opens DevTools, and every visitor would spend one of your API calls.

Instead, put a small endpoint in front of your price provider and cache the result. This example uses Express and the fetch built into Node.js 18 and later:

Three things keep this endpoint dependable:

On the page, the loadSpot() function from Step 3 fills the field and shows the time of the price. The field stays editable, so a seller who has a quote from a specific buyer can type that instead.

A seller comparing offers might want to send their numbers to a family member, or come back to them tomorrow. Because every input has a name, turning the form into a query string is one line with URLSearchParams.

The syncUrl() function in Step 3 runs on every change and uses history.replaceState instead of pushState, so typing doesn't fill the back button with dozens of entries. On load, restoreFromUrl() puts the values back. A link like this opens with the form already filled in:

This is also the progressive enhancement story. If JavaScript fails to load, the form still submits as a GET request. Your server can read the same parameters, import the same gold.js and render the result in HTML.

Because goldValue() is a pure function, testing it needs no browser and no mocks. Node.js ships with a built-in test runner, so there's nothing to install:

Run it with node --test. (Add "type": "module" to your package.json so Node treats the files as ES modules.) The troy ounce test is the one worth keeping forever: if anyone "simplifies" the conversion later, it fails immediately.

A quick checklist for putting this calculator on a real store:

A gold calculator looks like a ten-line script, but the details are what make it useful: converting troy ounces properly, separating melt value from payout, keeping the math testable and making the result accessible and shareable. The same pattern of a pure calculation module, a thin DOM layer and a cached server endpoint works for any calculator where the price depends on several inputs, from shipping estimates to currency conversion.

Mathematically, 14K is 14 ÷ 24 = 58.3%. Many manufacturers stamp 14K jewelry "585" and alloy it to that standard, so both numbers are common. Pick one, state it in the dropdown, and use it consistently.

Let the user choose. Most people weigh jewelry in grams, but spot prices are quoted per troy ounce, so the calculator should accept either and convert internally.

Yes. Drop Step 4 and let users type the spot price, or have a scheduled job write the current price into a static JSON file. Everything else runs entirely in the browser.

#10639. Uber Eats driver saves elderly woman after hearing cries for help behind front door

An Uber Eats driver in Massachusetts helped save an elderly woman after hearing her faint cries for help while attempting to complete a delivery.

Brandon McSorley had started delivering orders through Uber Eats to earn extra money ahead of the holiday season when he received an order from a customer in Carver on November 22.

The delivery took him to Cranberry Village, a residential community for people aged 55 and older, where he noticed something was wrong after arriving at the customer’s home.

McSorley told CBS News that the woman had ordered Tylenol and ginger ale. Because the delivery contained medication, he was required to verify the customer’s ID before handing over the order.

However, the house was dark when he arrived, and nobody answered the door. After waiting several minutes and attempting to contact the customer, he began hearing noises from inside the residence.

“I could hear, like, a faint calling. I thought it was potentially someone telling me to go away or something like that,” he said.

McSorley remained outside until the woman’s cries became clearer, allowing him to hear her asking for help after suffering a fall. He immediately called 911 and waited for emergency services to arrive.

First responders transported the woman to a nearby hospital. According to Carver EMS, she had been lying on the floor for approximately 45 minutes without access to a phone or a medical alert device.

Carver EMS Chief Michael Ryan credited the delivery driver’s actions with preventing the woman from potentially spending much longer on the floor.

“A little voice in his head was telling him something was wrong here, and he followed up on it,” Ryan told CBS News. “From what I understand, she is expected to make a full recovery.”

Speaking to WCVB 5, McSorley said he was grateful that his delivery had brought him to the woman’s home when it did.

“Just, right place at the right time. I’m glad I could be there and really do something to help.”

It’s not clear how big of a tip McSorley received from the whole ordeal, but he surely earned a five-star review.
